# Executive Summary 

###### Uncertainty the only certainty 

- Our view of the fundamentals has shifted slightly since the last quarterly.  We are now expecting that refined consumption will be higher in 2012 but lower in 2013 than we did in April, mainly in China due to scrap market effects.  This is on top of our continued assumption o

f an acceleration in consumption growth in H2 in China, as economic policy is loosened and infrastructure focused stimulus measures boost copper end-use demand. 

- With refined production forecast to be higher than three months ago in both 2012 and 2013, our deficit forecast for this year has been trimmed to below 500,000t and the April forecast of a 150,000t deficit next year has been converted into a balanced market. 

- When looked at on a China/World ex-China basis in 2012 the picture is one of a surplus in the former and a deficit in the latter.  The small Chinese surplus comes from lower imports in H2 creating a deficit in the period to reduce the excess stocks built up in Q1.  An annual deficit of over 600,000t in the World ex-China was assured when Q1 alone saw a deficit of almost 570,000t.  Record Chinese cathode imports in Q1 this year were supplied by imports from all major producing countries, suggesting that producers drew down stocks. 

- For their part, investors have turned bearish due to on-going concerns over the Eurozone crisis and the economic outlook in general.  As a result, they sold copper and other commodities over the past three months.  Both fundamental and financial factors have come together to reduce the 2012 price forecast to just under $8,000/t ($3.60/lb). 

- In 2013, as the Chinese economy accelerates and the macroeconomic picture is expected to improve in the rest of the world, we forecast that the price will rise to an average of $8,500/t ($3.85/lb), peaking in Q2 before drifting lower through H2. 

- World consumption growth is forecast to peak in 2014.  With some mine projects shifted into later years, refined production will grow by less than consumption, tipping the market back into a small deficit.  In 2015 and 2016, rapidly rising output from mine projects will boost refined supply and the market will move into a period of sustained surplus.  As stocks increase the price will come down to an annual average below $7,350/t ($3.33/lb) by 2016.

###### **Major changes since the April 2012 Quarterly report** 

**Demand** : Upward revisions to North American and European 2011 consumption have been offset by downward shifts to South & Central America (C&SA) and Other Asia.  In 2012 the forecast has been raised by 150,000t due to the base effect of a higher 2011 in North America and Europe, as well as more consumption in China, which are offset only marginally by lower base effects in C&SA and Other Asia.  For 2013, Chinese and North American consumption have been revised down due to scrap effects, leaving a 115,000t lower total figure.  We have a cumulative 275,000t higher consumption forecast for 20142016, almost wholly due to higher Chinese consumption growth. 

**Supply** : Further upward revisions to 2011 mine output mean that refined production is 220,000t higher than previously estimated.  Potential refined production has been lowered in 2012 but higher mine production means that the actual forecast output is 220,000t above the April level.  More mine production in 2013 and 2015-16 is only minimally offset by a 150,000t reduction in 2014 output due to shifting forward of some probable and possible projects, leaving a cumulative 265,000t increase in refined output between 2013 and 2016. 

**Prices** : Prices for 2012 have been lowered by another $550/t and by $690/t in 2013 as a result of a slower decline in stocks to critically low levels and lower investor buying.  The reduction in price is not as great in 2014-16, ranging from $370/t lower in 2015 and only $150/t in 2016, as stocks rise to similar levels forecast in the April report. 

###### Macroeconomic outlook remains in the driving seat 

We forecast that the copper market will be in a deficit of almost 500,000t in 2012, as mine and refined production growth will be minimal compared to a more than 3% increase in consumption. The macroeconomic picture, and therefore copper consumption prospects, is at a critical juncture in the economic cycle, due to the Eurozone crisis and questions about Chinese and US growth prospects.  As a result, uncertainty over the direction of the economy is overshadowing copper fundamentals, as well as dictating the ebb and flow of sentiment among financial players.  The only fundamentals that have affected prices recently, and which we expect to continue to do so in the near term, are the relatively low levels of exchange stocks. 

The twists and turns of the copper price in May and June exemplify the impact of these factors on the market.  The 3-month price on the LME fell to a low for the year of $7,270/t on 8<sup>th</sup> June from a recent high of $8,440/t on 1<sup>st</sup> May.  The May high and subsequent decline was due in part to the backwardation that followed the largest ever one day cancellation of warrants on the LME on 20<sup>th</sup> April.  The cancellation was rumoured to be the work of a large trader and is reported to have caught Chinese smelters short.  They responded by exportin

g cathode to LME warehouses in Asia in May and early June, helping to achieve record monthly exports in May of 102,375t. 

Another apparent anomaly in the trade data was the fact that US imports into China reached a new record amount of over 30,000t of cathode in May.  This followed a then record US monthly import of almost 16,000t in April and in turn was followed by over 18,000t arriving from the US in June.  These shipments help explain the drawdown in exchange stocks in the US in Q1. However, the large negative arbitrage meant that someone suffered a high opportunity cost. 

The price also fell by the beginning of June as investors took a cautious approach and moved money into “safer” assets than copper as they awaited the outcome of the latest Greek election.  In the end the results of the Greek election were as positive as could be expected and the copper price

As a result, febrile sentiment switched rapidly into "risk on" mode, with the 3-month price on the LME jumping to a recent trading high of $7,819/t by 3<sup>rd</sup> July. 

###### China semis growth drives stronger copper consumption 

With stocks relatively low and refined supply growth constrained until projects begin to significantly raise mine output next year, the focus of attention in analysing the near term fundamentals is on the demand side.  In this context, China’s potential economic growth is the key driver.  Semis production growth was up by an estimated 16.2% y-o-y in H1 2012, but was down 0.5% on H2 2011.  The decline in prices in Q2 and the negative SHFE-LME arbitrage discouraged scrap imports, which decreased by 3.0% y-o-y based on our contained copper estimate.  However, scrap held back by traders in Q4 as a result of the decline in the copper price in October seems to have been released in H1 2012.  This led to real consumption of refined metal growing by “only” 11% y-o-y but falling by 3.8% on H2 2011, while scrap grew by an estimated 8.6% on H2 2011. 

On the economy front, the slowdown engineered in economic growth over the past year in China has contained the property bubble that had developed as a result of stimulus spending in 2008-2009.  However, the property market remains a cause for concern for the authorities, as property prices in the large cities have not fallen as much as in rural areas.  Therefore, the central government, as it continues to loosen monetary policy following the successful reining in of inflationary pressure, will seek to control lending by limiting credit to property but relaxing it for other sectors.  Interest rates for benchmark deposit rates and lending rates have already been reduced and the June data on bank lending show that it has increased relative to May.  These looser monetary conditions mean that the collateral stock trade, in which investors use copper as a financing tool to circumvent limits on credit, has been reduced.  Nevertheless, stocks in bonded warehouses remain elevated as imports fell in June, but imports are still above the monthly average level required to meet the shortfall in supply from domestic refineries.

In addition, the government is targeting infrastructure development for a round of stimulus spending that will be supportive. The announcement of subsidies for energy efficient home appliances and fuel efficient cars will only have a marginal impact on copper demand. The subsidies introduced in 2009 and sustained through last year brought forward too much demand for appliances for the latest subsidies to promote large scale additional buying by consumers. As industrial production growth accelerates from 9.7% y-o-y in Q2 to 12.6% by Q4 and the above policy measures feed through, we expect copper consumption in China to pick up sequentially in H2 2012. We forecast that refined consumption will rise from 1.9Mt in Q1 to 2.1Mt by the final quarter of the year and register a 7.2% increase for the full year, versus the 6.3% that we forecast in the April Quarterly. In 2013, we expect that as the economic activity picks up, scrap availability will rise in countries that export to China. Higher use of scrap will lead to slightly slower growth in refined consumption in China of 6.0%, despite industrial production ticking up from 11.4% this year to 12.5% in 2013. ###### European consumption growth down… We forecast that refined copper consumption in the World ex-China will rise by 1.0% in 2012, before rising to only 2.1% in 2013. However, behind the headline figures, European growt

h is expected to be a drag on growth this year, after supporting consumption in 2011, with the rest of the world doing the opposite – supporting growth this year after limiting it in 2011. 

Europe and how it manages its twin banking and sovereign debt crises remains the largest single source of uncertainty about the demand outlook.  As we expected three months ago, conditions have deteriorated.  Northern countries are still doing much better than those in the south.  However, the momentum in the north has slowed as the seemingly interminable wrangling over debt reduction and austerity measures saps consumer and business confidence.  European businesses are dependent on bank financing and exposure of European banks in the north and the south to sovereign debt, and in the case of Spain property loans, means that end users are suffering a credit squeeze.  As a result, end users are finding it difficult to finance buying activities including of copper semis and copper containing end-use products.  Consequently, we forecast

that copper consumption will decline by 1.8% in 2012 in Western Europe.  We expect to see a continued “muddle through” approach to the crisis which means consumption in Western Europe will be lacklustre in 2013, growing by only 1.0%. 

In Eastern Europe, the underlying demand is not as strong as the regional growth rate of 2.5% for 2012 implies.  This aggregate rate includes Russia, which is seeing growing consumption as a result of the reintroduction of the cathode import tax last year.  The tax has boosted refined consumption, as wirerod is produced for export instead of shipping cathode directly.  Strip out Russia and the growth in the remainder of the region is negative to the tune of 2.0% this year, as the impact of the spillover effects of the Eurozone crisis holds back activity in the region.  A similar dichotomy persists into 2013, with regional growth of 3.2% driven by 4.6% in Russia versus only a 0.2% increase in the rest of the region. 

###### …but rest of World bounces back from 2011 decline 

As noted above, the rest of the world hindered growth in 2011 but is now bouncing back to support consumption this year.  Within this overall picture, the US has seen mixed developments over the past few months.  The new SDI-La Farga wirerod plant that began operation in June will be a drag on refined consumption in North America, as its production displaces that of other regional wirerod producers.  On the positive side, the auto sector continues to perform well, with Ford and Chrysler reporting that they will limit summer shutdowns at their plants to meet the sustained demand for new vehicles in the country.  However, the position of the all-important construction sector remains gloomy.  There have been some flickers of an upturn for several months, but the overhang of homeowners with negative equity is huge, as is the number of emp

ty homes.  Until these are cleared rates of growth in residential construction activity will remain subdued.  Overall, we expect that refined consumption will rise by 3.3% in the US, following last year’s 0.4% decline.  Next year, decelerating North American industrial production plus the full impact of the SDI-La Farga mill will lead to regional consumption declining by 1.6%. 

Central & South American refined consumption growth is on course to grow by 4.8% this year, as Brazil recovers from its downturn in 2011.  In 2013, Brazilian preparations for the World Cup in 2014 and Olympics in 2016 are expected to gather pace.  Therefore, copper consumption in the region will accelerate to 6.0%. 

With domestic growth subdued and semis capacity increases meaning China is taking fewer semis imports, refined copper consumption in the rest of Asia is suffering, particularly in the major exporters Taiwan and South Korea.  The Thai floods dragged down copper consumption in Other Asia last year, so the annual comparisons are resulting in growth, although for the year as a whole we forecast a modest rise of just 1.5%.  In Japan, subsidies for fuel efficient cars are boosting auto demand, including for copper.  The Japanese Electric Wire & Cable Makers’ Association reported that shipments to the auto sector rose by 36.3% y-o-y in June.  However, this is compared to the period of reduced auto production shortly following the March earthquake and tsunami last year and full year refined growth is forecast to be only 2.0%.  Next year a slow acceleration in industrial activity in both Japan and the rest of the Asian region will lead to only 3.2% refined consumption growth.

###### Uncertainty leaves investors on the sidelines 

Investors will continue to react very quickly to developments in the Eurozone crisis.  As a result, we have seen and will continue to see high levels of price volatility, which is not the ideal environment to encourage a longer-term commitment from commodity investors.  Instead, they will look for a clear sign of stability in the euro before having the confidence to commit their capital to the commodity sector in a significant way. 

Even though the Chinese economy will improve during the next six to nine months, which means that commodity demand is likely to gather momentum, the outlook also points to a stronger US dollar during that timeframe.  In fact, in the very short term, the uncertainty around the euro is so high that it is not clear how far it might decline before it finally stabilises.  Thus, potentially, any price gains in commodities that might occur due to stronger physical market fundamentals could be eliminated completely by a stronger US dollar.  This explains why commodity market investors remain on the sidelines, preferring to hold cash.  The comparative analysis of asset classes in Q2 2012 indicates that equities and bonds are not performing terribly well, either, so money is not moving from commodities to other places.  Rather, it’s waiting to find its next destination.

The range is wider than in previous quarterlies, as we have widened the bands to better reflect historical copper price ranges. Downside macroeconomic and financial risks and their consequent negative impact on consumption are offsetting the upside risks of lower copper production and higher investor inflows into copper. One point to note is that Chinese buying as the price falls below $7,000/t provides a floor for the price. In 2013, as the forecast is lower than in April, the risks remain symmetrical. From 2014 to 2016, the risks become biased to the high side, as production risks come to the fore, driven principally by production possibly underperforming compared to the base case. The downside risks come from demand significantly underperfo

rming the base through some form of intensified economic disruptions, most likely driven by another financial sector shock. 

###### **Production risks** 

Production risks to the price are mostly to the upside.  The first is that tight availability of equipment, qualified personnel, water, power, etc. mean that sequencing of projects (at both the company and industry levels) will be a serious challenge.  We believe that there is a greater downside than upside risk to our production forecast and therefore an upward bias to the price forecast, especially in the 2014-16 period, when there is significant risk that mine projects will not come on as expected in the base case. 

There is some downside risk from production.  We have a mine disruption allowance in the 2014-2016 period of 12-13% and have made allowances for project risks of a 10% underperformance for firm projects, 30% for probable and 60% for possible ones.  If our macroeconomic forecast turns out to be too optimistic, then demand could be less and the wave of mine projects could come on just in time to swamp the market and drive down prices sooner than in our base case. 

###### **Macroeconomic and financial risks** 

The key risk to the copper price is the uncertainty of how the global economy will perform. The apparent improvement in the US could prove short-lived and China could possibly not see a return to growth in H2 2012.  The Eurozone crisis could also still prompt more financial market

turmoil.  The safe haven status of the US dollar in a crisis could also see it strengthen faster than we have accounted for in the base case, which would be negative for a dollar denominated price. 

On the other hand, in the near term the continuing tightness in the forward curve shows that there could be another squeeze engineered. The resulting move into backwardation at the front end of the forward curve could lead to a higher price outturn than in our base case.  In addition, economic growth in both the US and China could prove stronger than forecast in the base case. This would be positive for growth in these important consuming countries, but also in those emerging markets which export to these two large economies.  It would also provide a spur to investors to boost holdings of risk assets such as copper. 

###### **Consumption risks** 

###### **Downside** 

Aluminium producers are currently facing challenging conditions, with the industry in a situation of chronic oversupply.  Smelter closures began in the beginning of 2012, with many of the closures directly impacting captive hot metal wirerod plants at aluminium smelters.  So, despite a Cu:Al price ratio of almost 4:1, supply constraints are likely to prevent aluminium from increasing its market share in the rod sector in the short term.  Longer term though, the substitution threat remains significant for copper demand growth in wirerod.  W

e expect aluminium will make more inroads into the insulated power cable market as a result of an increase in aluminium wirerod capacity available to target this segment by 2015. 

CRU forecasts that the ratio of the copper price to that of aluminium will average close to 4:1, which will weigh on all consumers’ strategic decision-making regarding substituting away from copper. 

###### **Upside** 

The potential shortage of scrap for direct use (due to weaker generation) could lead to additional cathode requirements, especially in China. 

A double-dip recession would only accelerate the emerging markets decoupling their economic growth further from the industrialised countries by favouring copper-intensive domestic demand. 

Some Chinese consumers or the SRB could see copper as a bargain for speculative purposes at prices much lower than our base case, thus leading to higher cathode imports.  As a result of RMB appreciation, further support for copper could also emerge from a diversion of surplus cash away from the dollar and directly into commodity investments as a means of diversification.

The continuing debt-crisis in Europe and slower economic growth in China has led to some very negative sentiment on the prospects for refined copper demand this year.  Our base case assumes that the European economy will not collapse nor worsen significantly and that China will meet its GDP growth target of 7.5% y-o-y in 2012.  In 2012, growth in copper cathode consumption will be driven by China, which is expected to rise by 7.2% y-o-y, supported by a relaxation in monetary policies, together with infrastructural and housing investment, targeted subsidies and a tightened scrap market at least until the end of Q3. 

North American copper demand has also been strong and we expect full year refined demand growth of 2.1% y-o-y, supported by growth in the US automotive industry, electrical infrastructure and industrial sectors.  However, this growth may have been greater without the rise in scrap usage in North America with the introduction of SDI-La Farga‟s new wirerod mill.

###### Distortions imposed by the scrap market 

Changes in copper semis demand can on the most part be reduced to the impact of changes in end use demand, as reflected by the close growth relationship it has with global industrial production growth.  However, copper cathode demand is more volatile and has a different growth pattern to end use demand.  The principal factor that distorts this relationship is the use of copper scrap in semis production.  We estimate that direct scrap usage in the copper semis fabrication industry accounted for 21% of total semis production in 2011.  Material availability differences in the cathode and copper scrap market means that relative usage varies from yearto-year, which often lead to much lower or higher refined copper consumption compared to changes in end-use demand. 

An important difference between the cathode and scrap supply is its price elasticity.  Copper cathode supply is relatively price inelastic compared to copper scrap supply.  A change in the rel

evant metal exchange‟s copper spot delivery price therefore has different effects upon copper cathode and copper scrap availability. Copper cathode availability does not respond to changes in the price level very much as most consumers are hedged and pass the costs downstream. However, copper scrap availability responds very rapidly to changes in the price level because there is a larger proportion of scrap merchants who are exposed to changes in the price. When the copper price falls, they are left with „expensive‟ material which is stocked until the price rises once again. When the price rises they release those expensive stocks until the price falls or the stocks are depleted. The effect of this is that changes in copper scrap prices tend to be less than changes in copper cathode prices. This means that in a rising copper price scenario, scrap supply is good, and the widening price difference from cathode means that it is favourable for CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly July 2012 Chapter 1 17 consumption. In a declining price environment cathode demand tends to be supported as scrap becomes scarcer. Refined copper consumption

International trade in copper scrap tends to exaggerate the change in scrap availability due to price changes. There is trade data to suggest that China, as a major importer of scrap, has encountered this phenomenon a number of times. The copper price had been on an upward trend from 2009 to early-2011 but then collapsed in October 2011. Whilst prices rose in 2010, merchants imported growing amounts of scrap resulting in the level of scrap availability rising and resulting in a 61% stimulated rise in scrap and alloy metal consumption in H2 2010 compared to H1. However, the copper price peaked in February and continued a downward (albeit volatile) trend through to Q4 2011 when it collapsed to below US$7,000/t. This squeezed the scrap market, as merchants withdrew any imports purchased at a higher price and scrap consumption decreased by an estimated 24% and 19% period-on-period in H1 and H2 2011. Imports of copper scrap over this period still remained at similar levels to the previous year. Since the level of consumption of high grade scrap and alloy material was falling, but copper scrap import volumes remained at a high level and at an equivalent grade, scrap merchants stockpiles must have grown considerably. As prices rose in Q1 scrap merchant stocks were made available once again, loosening the scrap market but seeing to a large rise in scrap and alloy metal consumption of an estimated 68% q-oq, despite the weaker semis demand associated with the Spring Festival early in Q1. As copper prices recovered slightly in Q2, the scrap market again tightened and scrap consumption responded accordingly, dropping 17% in Apr-May on the previous two-month period. ###### **3.2.1 Western Europe** 

We are currently undertaking a thorough study of our historical figures for copper cathode consumption in Western Europe. As such, this issue‟s country analysis shall focus upon growth rates and trends rather than absolute consumption levels, which are likely to change due to our targeted programme of work. 

Continuing on from the poor H2 2011, Western European refined copper consumption picked up by only 0.5% period-on-period to reach 1.41Mt in H1 2012. ###### **3.3.1 North East Asia** 

Activity of the copper consuming industries in South Korea and Taiwan was lower than expected in 2011. We attribute this to the migration of Taiwanese cablemakers to mainland China, increasing the Chinese market for semi-finished products and (if the cablemaker opts to procure wirerod locally) also increasing the Chinese market for refined or scrap copper. The South Korean downstream copper industry has

encountered many of the same structural phenomena as Taiwan (although to a lesser extent relative to cathode market size) impacting our estimates of refined copper consumption within the nation. The key exception is that there is no marked migration trend of South Korean wire and cable or copper semi-fabricators toward China. Exports of semi-finished products, however, still comprised 15.4% of total semis production in 2010. This figure fell in 2011 to 11.7% representing a reduction of around 60,000t. 48,000t of this y-o-y loss was attributable to a decline in semis exports to China. Aside from losses associated with Korea‟s export market, we attribute a decline of around 30,000t in 2011 to weakness in the construction sector, activity in which contracted by 6% y-o-y and overshadowed growth in South Korea‟s automotive production. In 2012, we expect to see more declines in refined copper consumption in Taiwan and South Korea. Growth in output of Chinese semi-fabricated products is not expected to be as significant as 2011 and another rise in China‟s semis capacity, particularly with reference to flat rolled products, will result in greater import substitution of Taiwanese and South Korean exports in favour of domestic production. On the bright side for South Korea, macroeconomic CRU International Limited confidential 28 Copper Quarterly July 2012 Chapter 1 indicators suggest that underlying domestic demand for copper this year has not worsened, so the fall in cathode consumption ought to be slower than in 2011. The rate of decline in Taiwan, on the other hand, will be greater than in South Korea, reflecting Taiwan‟s greater exposure to China and expectations of less potential for upside in its domestic market. In the previous issue of the Copper Quarterly, we reported that Japan‟s semis industry growth was on course to meet our cathode consumption growth forecast of +2% y-o-y.  Output of brass mill products, which is larger than the copper wire and cable industry by gross weight, was down by 8.8% y-o-y in Q1 2012.  However, we anticipated a pick-up in the y-o-y rate in Q2 and Q3 due to impact of the 11<sup>th</sup> March earthquake and tsunami upon the automotive industry in 2011. 

The actual brass mills semis production figures in Japan indicate that there was no positive swing in the y-o-y growth rate, instead, growth turned negative, averaging -9.2% y-o-y for April and May 2012 (67,815t and 65,320t, respectively).  The underperformance was limited to brass mill semi-fabricated products, as Japanese wire mill volumes grew by 3.1% y-o-y in the corresponding months (31,768t and 27,861t, respectively).  Data released by the **Japan Copper and Brass Association** indicates that the contraction in brass mill semis production was not limited to a single semis product but affected almost the entire range.  Notable declining products are those with the largest volumes, copper and brass sheet and strip.  Breaking down

###### **3.3.2 China** 

Demand for copper in China remained subdued throughout H1 2012.  As reported in the previous issue, the usual sustained growth in copper demand following the Chinese Lunar New Year did not occur.  This was partially as a consequence of the less pronounced seasonal dip in refined consumption during the holiday month but was also related to weaker y-o-y growth in underlying economic activity.  Industrial production expanded by 11.6% y-o-y in Q1, slowing from the rate of growth seen in the same period of the previous year of 14.8% y-o-y. Furthermore, IP growth slowed again in Q2, registering 9.7% y-o-y, the weakest growth performance in China since Q2 2009.  Fixed asset investment statistics from the National Bureau of Statistics of China indicate strong overall growth of 20.1% year-to-date for Jan-May 2012, supporting copper demand.  Interest rate cuts in June and July, as well as a reduction in banks reserve ratio and the introduction of new stimulus policies, promise faster growth for period-on-period copper consumption in H2 2012.  This has already impacted the manufacturing sector, July PMI‟s for which showed renewed activity after 5 months of contraction.

Copper semis-fabricators have been relatively downbeat about conditions and demand in Q2 of this year.  GDP growth predictions were steadily revised downwards toward 7.5% y-o-y and semis fabricators felt the pinch as order rates and facility operating rates both fell.  The CNIA reported copper semis production (by gross weight, including a CRU estimate for June 2012) was down by 0.5% period-on-period in H1 2012.  This is not unusual; there was a more significant decline from H2 to H1 last year and the slight decline seen this year still includes a pick-up with the onset of the second quarter of semis-production, rising by 16% q-o-q in Q2, which is again, a normal seasonal trend.  Market participants‟ dismay appears to be linked to the more marked fall in cathode consumption.  After accounting for bonded warehouse and exchange stock changes, apparent consumption of copper cathode fell by 10% in H1 on H2 2011.  After considering stock changes at producers, consumers and other off-warrant locations, we estimate that cathode consumption was down by 3.8% y-o-y in H1, representing an u

nprecedented decline for a half-year in China. However, this is only one side of the equation. As cathode consumption decreased, the usage of copper scrap and alloying metal grew by 8.6% period-on-period in H1 2012. The primary factor driving this change was price dynamics. The collapse and subsequent volatility in prices, which began in late September 2011, initiated scrap-stocking behaviour, constricting supply and tightening the market. This was especially true in China whose copper industry relies heavily upon trade of scrap to meet demand. In periods of good scrap availability at neutral prices, we have observed that incoming copper-in-scrap equals between 50 to 65% of the total scrap and alloy material consumption in semis production. In H2 2011, this figure rose to 94%, as import volumes in terms of copper content were sustained but scrap and alloy consumption declined by 19% on H1 as scrap merchants opted to stock material. Refined copper consumption grew in response, increasing by 16.9% in the period. In 2012, prices began to climb once more, encouraging scrap stockists to sell their supplies, loosening the market, widening scrap discounts and leading to heightened scrap and alloy metal consumption in place of demand for the more expensive copper cathode. Copper-in-scrap imported volumes have contracted, mainly due to a drop in their implied grade (unit price vs. LME price with one quarter lag). Additionally, scrap and alloy consumption was rising in Q2 compared to Q1 and Q2 2011 (up by 27% q-o-q and 13% y-o-y, respectively) as the copper price traded within a narrower range; mitigating chances for scrap supply constraints. Increasing competition from the US for high grade scrap and poor industrial development in Europe have both led to poor availability of higher grade scrap to China, resulting in the aforementioned drop in implied grade. This has helped to lift refined copper consumption, which, while underperforming semis growth may rise more quickly if scrap tradeflows are further constrained, especially as stocks of scrap in China have already been drawndown significantly in the year so far. The Chinese

copper fabrication industry has also been contending with increasing competition and the associated rise in industry production capacity.  As total copper consumption has been weaker than expected, there has been divergence between the rate of industry expansion and the rate of orders, impacting on operating rates.  Statistics on utilisation rates tend to differ substantially depending on the type of semis products it considers and also the diversity of the survey group.  For example, in April, we heard that large fabricators had not experienced as severe a drop in operating rates as their smaller capacity rivals.  Larger fabricators tend to be State-owned enterprises and have the capability to handle big public sector contracts.  This position has allowed them to take advantage of new investment in the power and social housing sectors, which continued to be major sources of support for the copper products manufacturers as growth in the economy slowed.  In H1 2012, it was quite clear that operating rates in general had decreased, but there were considerable differences between semis-fabricators of different product type.  The **China Nonferrous Metals Fabrication Industrial Association** (CNFA) recently reported that there are in excess of 3Mt/y of semis projects expected to come on-stream in the 2011-15 period, of which 1.5Mt/y are wirerod mills, 1.2Mt/y are flat rolled products and 450,000t/y are copper tubes, bars and shapes. 

In April, Antaike reported that, of all copper semis producers, it was copper tube manufacturers that were experiencing the best utilisation rates after the end of the Spring Festival holiday in January.  Their survey, which was performed in February, showed that utilisation rates had been rising and mostly ranged between 75% - 80%.  The data also said that the median copper rod plant operating rate was around 75%, whereas copper plate, sheet and strip (PSS) utilisation rates were notably lower at under 70%.  The copper tube industry has matured and has approximately matched capacity to demand as it has consolidated into a number of large companies.  In contrast to this, the copper PSS industry is relatively young, with domestic production beginning in earnest around 2006.  As such, the industry remains fragmented and capacity is being installed at a furious pace, leaving participants vulnerable to any weakness in end use demand.  The addition of 1.2Mt of annual copper PSS capacity before 2015, as the CNFA forecasts, is very likely to occur in CRU‟s opinion.  Research shows that at least 480,000t of capacity was installed between Q1 2011 and Q1 2012 (+19% y-o-y), which raises our estimate of total flat rolled copper capacity in China to 3Mt/y.  We estimate that consumption of copper flat rolled products grew by only 5% y-o-y in Q1 2012.  This implies that the mean average utilisation rate is likely to have fallen below 60% as of the end of Q1

Some officials believe that previous subsidies have already tapped all potential extra demand for home appliances.  The waning effect of the rural stimulus certainly seems to support this theory as the **Ministry of Commerce** reported that sales volume under that subsidy scheme fell by 5.7% y-o-y in the first five months of 2012 to reach just over 30M units. However the lagged effects on copper products manufacturing, together with high of inventory levels of air conditioners and automobiles, means that the impact on refined copper consumption will largely be felt in 2013. 

A positive factor for copper demand both in H2 2012 and in the medium term comes from the railway sector.  The Ministry of Railways is trying to restart plans to build-out 85 urban railway lines across more than 30 cities with a total length of 2,700km by 2015.  The ministry had shelved the plans following the withdrawal of central government‟s funding for the projects following the high-speed train crash tragedy that took place on 23<sup>rd</sup> July 2011.  However, the ministry has since introduced measures to raise funds by itself: RMB20B through issuance of a bond and also a RMB2.0 trillion credit line, which was granted by banks last year.  It is therefore likely that the rail sector will become the largest driver of growth in the coming years. In addition to this, reports from early July indicated that the ministry had only spent RMB148B of an annual railway budget worth RMB448B, leaving room for a significant boost in copper consumption for H2 2012.  As of early May, the ministry reported that it had 96 urban rail lines under construction in 16 cities with a total operating length of 2,200km.  In recent years, railway transport construction has averaged 270km per annum. 

Our outlook with regards to the power infrastructure and social housing sectors of demand remain the same as reported in the previous issue of the Copper Quarterly.  We expect power infrastructure development, as the State Grid invests in extending the power grid to inland cities.  This will boost refined copper consumption but will not drive it because as most of the work appears to involve power transmission projects, which are areas of lower copper intensity than power distribution. **Antaike** reported in April that copper consumption in the power sector is expected to rise by 7.1% y-o-y in 2012, supporting refined copper growth.  The outlook fo

r the social housing project this year remains unclear, as local government funding could still be a bottle-neck.  Should the 23% budgetary increase that we reported in the April issue be sufficient, then the plan of completing 5M social housing units this year is likely to be executed. This would boost copper demand significantly compared to 2011, which was more heavily focused on the lower copper intensity housing starts rather than housing completions. 

Overall, our view of refined copper consumption in China is for strengthening growth in the second half of 2012 as the easing of monetary tightening policies improves underlying end use in private consumer sectors, including autos and home appliances.  Additional growth from end use trends are expected to materialise from H2-weighted investment in the railway transport sector and also increases in copper tonnages associated with social housing construction completions.  It remains to be seen how the private construction sector responds to the eased monetary policy, we have included only a slight improvement in this sector, as idled construction project find sufficient funding to be completed.  On top of these factors, if the copper price continues the same sideways but volatile trend as we have seen in the first half of the year then the scrap market is likely to tighten.  This is because we believe that stocks of scrap are already very thin in China and overseas supply is expected to remain weak due to increased high grade demand in North America and poor generation in Europe.  This would therefore act to support elevated growth of refined copper cathode consumption through the remainder of the year.

Having already seen cathode consumption of 3.9Mt in H1 2012 in China, representing growth of 11.2% y-o-y or -3.9% on H2 2011, we expect acceleration in refined copper demand in the second half.  H2 2012 is forecast to see consumption of 4.2Mt, up by 3.7% y-o-y and 7.9% on H1.  Refined copper demand for full year 2012 therefore amounts to 8.2Mt, up by 7.2% y-o-y. In 2013, the underlying end-use demand promises for improvement on 2012.  This is mainly due to our expectation that there will be a rise in manufactured export goods and domestic consumerism.  However, despite this, we expect refined copper demand growth to slow to 6.0% y-o-y due to our view that the scrap market will loosen significantly as a result of an upward price trend and improved scrap supply from Europe due to improving economic conditions. 2014 and 2015 will see a cyclical acceleration in copper cathode consumption of 7.8% y-o-y and 6.5% y-o-y, as underlying demand remains strong on the back of accelerated investment in the social housing, power and railway sectors to meet performance targets set out in the 12<sup>th</sup> Five Year Plan.  Additionally, we expect a tightening scrap market in these years (supporting copper cathode demand gro

wth) as the copper price is expected to fall due to expanding refined copper production.  After 2015, underlying copper demand is expected to wane as economic growth in China becomes increasingly dependent upon private consumption in the place of investment and exports, putting a lower ceiling on the potential rate of annual growth in copper demand.   By this point, we expect China to be self-sufficient in semi-fabricated products. Infrastructural growth in terms of copper intensity would be driven by railway investment and power.  We expect growth of around 6.4% y-o-y, with the rate of cathode demand slowing as the forecast moves into the longer term beyond the forecast horizon.

###### 1. Key points 

- Mine output is expected to increase by 0.2% in 2012 to 16.2Mt.  We have adjusted our annual production number upwards by around 200,000t compared to our estimate of 16.0Mt in the April Quarterly. 

- In Q2 2012, seven new copper projects started up.  The largest of these was the Salobo I project in Brazil with an estimated production capacity of 100,000t of copper-inconcentrate after ramping up. 

- A large number of new projects are expected to come on stream in 2013, which will mark the start of a period of expansion in global mine production with annual growth rates in aggregate production of 4-7% until 2016. 

- Mining operations and projects under development have faced increasing obstacles from governments in the last couple of years and there were further developments in Q2 as several countries around the world have announced major changes to their mining codes, which include higher royalties and restrictions on exports.  There has also been growing opposition to mining from local communities due to environmental concerns   Protests and demonstrations have been frequent in South America, in Peru especially. 

- We estimate that smelter production reached 3.40Mt of copper-in-blister in Q2 2012, up by 5.2% from Q1 2012 and a 1.9% increase y-o-y. Additionally, smelters have become somewhat cautious in light of uncertain future Chinese refined copper demand.

quality concentrate intensified, with TC/RCs for the latter falling to low levels as a result of increased demand for blending. - The copper scrap market became very tight in Q2 in light of many scrap merchants opting to withhold material from the market following a drop in refined copper prices. The tight scrap market put some downward pressure on TC/RCs for concentrate, as some smelters turned to it as a substitute. Overview Total mine production in 2012 will amount to 16.2Mt of contained copper, a 0.2% increase compared to 2012. We have adjusted our annual production number upwards by around 200,000t compared to our estimate of 16.0Mt in the April Quarterly. Conversely, because of project delays, we have reduced the expected production in 2013 by 60,000t to 17.2Mt and revised down the expected production in 2014 by 220,00t to 17.9Mt. Nevertheless, we maintain that mine production will increase significantly over the coming years. Labour unrest** In line with the first quarter of the year, there were very few labour-related disruptions in Q2 2012. The most important developments include a two-day strike by contract workers at Escondida, a two-day strike by workers at Kazakhmys’ Annensky operation, reports of additional strike threats at the Grasberg mine, a 10-day strike at Doe Run Peru’s Cobriza mine in Peru and a one-day general strike by Peruvian miners. The decrease in labour-related disruptions is mainly due to that fact that fewer labour contracts are up for negotiation this year. The risk of strikes will increase towards the end of the year, as labour contracts at several mining operations are due to expire. Contract workers at the Escondida mine laid down

tools and staged a partial blockade of the mine on May 2nd and 3rd in a dispute with the management over bonuses. Unionized workers did not join in the strike and the blockade ended quickly, with the management announcing that it would review the demands of the workers and also adding that production had not been disrupted by the strike. Escondida had a very challenging 2011 with declining ore grades, a 14day strike and a drop in production of 25% that also forced the management to declare _force majeure_ on shipments. In 2012, the mine has been performing much better. As already mentioned, ore grades have recovered somewhat and there have been no significant labour related disruptions this year. Government issues** “Resource nationalism” on the part of certain governments has continued to pose challenges to the mining industry in Q2. The most important developments have been in Indonesia, where the government imposed a 20% tax on exports of ores. Meanwhile, the Chilean government has recently drafted a new law based on the ILO 169 Convention that establishes certain rules around the rights of indigenous people in terms of the use of their land. The government of Indonesia imposed a 20% tax on exports of ore that came into effect on 6th May 2012. The news comes after several announcements of new mining regulations earlier this year, including renegotiation of mining contracts and a regulation limiting foreign ownership of mining projects to 49%. The export tax aims to encourage investment in ore processing facilities that would add value to exports and boost Indonesia’s domestic industry. Companies that hold Contracts of Work (COW) agreements, including Freeport-McMoRan, Vale and Newmont are exempt from this new regulation. However, the government has expressed interest in renegotiating the COW agreements. The export tax preludes a planned ban on exports of unprocessed metal ores from 2014 and is intended to prevent a mine production boom prior to the ban coming into force. The miners are already required to have an export permit in order to export minerals and the government has asked all miners to develop and submit plans for downstream processing of ore as a requirement for issuing export permits. Mine production in Indonesia is expected to reach 470,000t of contained copper in 2012, but refined production is expected to be 260,000t with refined production capacity at 325,000t. Thus, just over half of Indonesia’s copper concentrate production is processed into refined copper domestically, with the majority of the remaining material shipped to smelters in Japan, India and China. Although there have been rumours of increasing investments in smelters, we have only heard of one concrete Indonesian smelting project in the pipeline with a refined copper production capacity of 200,000t/y, due for commencement in 2014. We anticipate that Indonesian mine production will more than double to around 1.03Mt/y of copper-in-concentrate by 2016 because of new projects. The government hopes that

this will create incentives for additional investment in smelting in order to bridge the gap between mine production and refined capacity.  However, most of the existing and future mine output, including output from projects, will come from Freeport-McMoRan’s and Newmont Mining’s operations, both purportedly protected by COW agreements.  Consequently, until further clarification, the new duty tax is more likely to deter future mining investment, rather than opening up new smelting and refining opportunities. 

The attempts by the Indonesian government to increase the degree of domestic processing are a reflection of a more general global trend.  In March, the government of the DRC had announced that it was contemplating similar export regulation.  The Zambian government also announced in April that it intends to ban the export of copper raw materials in an effort to add value to the domestic industry.  The Zambian President Michael Sata recently announced that he sees the production of the higher value-added copper and copper products as key for boosting the local economy.  CRU was in Zambia in June, and our impression is that there is currently a lot of focus on how the country can benefit more from its natural resources.  President Sata and many other commentators have highlighted that Zambia is plagued by high unemployment and poor infrastructure despite possessing very large deposits of copper and the high copper prices seen over the last couple of years.  A World Bank study also observed that; “Zambia needs to capture

However, the mining royalty was recently doubled to 6%.  The country would begin to appear more risky to investors if mineral taxes and royalties change too often.

The moratorium on mining applications was implemented in January 2011 to allow the government time to review its mining policy.  Following the completion of the policy review, the government said that the first step towards lifting the moratorium was an executive order issued by Philippines’ president Benigno Aquino III on July 9<sup>th</sup> requiring local mining regulation to be consistent with national laws. Although their opinions on the project will not be legally binding they will feed into the SEA’s assessment and will influence its outcome.  The proposed framework bears some similarities to that already in place in Peru. 

###### **2.2.4. Environmental issues** 

The environmental impact of mining continues to be the main reason for opposition to mining projects from local communities.  In May, protesters in Peru were campaigning against alleged environmental pollution from Xstrata’s Tintaya mine and Antapaccay project and demanding that Xstrata pays the local government a greater share of its profits.  During the week-long protest, two people were killed and around 50 were injured.  The government of President Ollanta Humala in Peru was forced to suspend freedom of assembly rights in order to break up protests and roadblocks surrounding the operations.  Xstrata reported that operations were proceeding as normal, with good stocks of concentrate at its port ready for shipment. Production is in the process of being phased out at the 120,000t/y Tintaya copper mine, with the neighbouring 160,000t/y copper-in-concentrate Antapaccay project set to commence production in August 2012.

Mutanda and Kanuaki will subsequently reimburse Katanga Mining so that the investment cost is shared equally between the three mines. The agreement has not yet been finalized, as some of the conditions set out have yet to be satisfied. 

MMG’s Kinsevere operation in the DRC was also affected by power failure, which forced ramping-up operations to be rescheduled and production to slow down.  The company has already replaced the four electricity transformers in the electro-winning circuit at the plant and temporary diesel generators were installed on site in June as a short-term solution to the power problem.  This is likely to increase the costs of the operation.  MMG has announced that it expects to produce 28,000t-32,000t of EW cathode in 2012, depending on power supply.  The company is also pursuing longer-term solutions to the power problem, and has acquired a larger share of peak electricity from the national electricity provider in the DRC.  The company has also been negotiating with the Zambian state power company ZESCO to access additional power supplies across the border.   However, in Zambia too, power outages have been a frequent problem in the past. 

We have not heard of any reports of infrastructure-related disruptions to mine production in Q2 2012.  Nevertheless, miners are well aware of the fact that power supply will be one of the key challenges to future mine projects.  In particular, low ore grades of new mining projects imply that more ore processed per tonne of copper, which means that energy requirements are already growing. 

Until recently, First Quantum had refused to begin construction of the Sentinel copper project in Zambia unless an agreement was reached with Zambia’s state owned electricity supplier, ZESCO, on an electricity tariff level.  However, after an agreement was reached the board of directors of First Quantum Minerals approved the construction of the project.  An NI 43-101 technical report on the Sentinel project, released by First Quantum on 9<sup>th</sup> May, stated that talks with ZESCO “confirm that power costs will actually be $0.075/kWh”.

Q2 is usually the “marejada” season in Chile, when the sea levels rise, potentially causing problems for seaports and shipping.  Last year, the situation was particularly bad with ports forced to close for several days and miners having to reschedule shipments.  This year, however, shipping has been unaffected by this phenomenon. 

Looking ahead, Q3 is the winter season in Chile and heavy snowfall could potentially cause disruptions to mining operations, particularly in the Andes.  September is usually the time of the El Nino.  The El Nino does not usually affect mining operations directly; however, it can potentially have indirect effects.  Agricultural activity is highly dependent on the El Nino and the associated rainy season, but changing weather patterns have been causing difficulties for farmers.  Since mining has often been associated with climate changes, the occurrence or lack of the El Nino can potentially shift the general public attitude towards mining and therefore affect the degree of local opposition to mining operations.

Mine projects have continued to suffer from delays and obstacles to development over the last quarter, with increased resource nationalism, concern over environmental issues and local opposition to development becoming major factors in addition to rising CAPEX, the shortage of skilled workers and supplies and technical challenges. The main developments are summarised below and full stories can be found in Appendix B of this report. Early May saw the first case in recent history where a local community has halted the development of a large mine project. The environmental permit for the El Morro copper-gold project in Chile was suspended following a filing by the Comunidad Agricola Los Huasco Altinos (CAHA) which stated that the community had not been sufficiently consulted over the effects of the project as stated by the International Labour Organisation (ILO) 169 Convention on Indigenous and Tribal Peoples (enacted in 1989). CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly July 2012 Chapter 2 55 Since the ruling, construction activities have ceased at the project site, and the project’s owners are currently working closely with the SEA to comply with the requirements of the ILO 169 Convention. It could take about 18 months to resume development work, according to local press reports. Following the suspension of the project, the head of CAHA said that it will claim consultation for other projects, including the Relincho (Teck), Pachuy (Barrick Gold) and Paso de la Flecha projects. He also said that it will avoid the involvement of NGOs. Other copper mine projects in the region are Pascua Lama (Barrick Gold), Caserones (Lumina Copper) and Cerro Casale (Barrick Gold, Kinross Gold) which could also be exposed to a similar situation. The development of Barrick Gold’s bi-national Pascua Lama gold, silver and copper project located on the Chile-Argentine border has encountered a setback after the Argentine National Supreme Court overturned a preliminary injunction issued by a local government which permitted the project to go ahead despite not conforming to all terms of the 2010 National Glacier Protection Act. The National Glacier Act prohibits any mining activities taking place in close proximity to glacial and p

eriglacial areas.  Barrick Gold maintains that the permit it received from the San Juan local government is legally binding and that it intends to continue construction work in spite of the Supreme Court’s ruling.  Although the Pascua Lama project has a relatively small copper production capacity, the decision of the Argentine National Supreme Court may set a precedent for more significant copper developments in the region, in particular Xstrata’s 280,000t/y contained copper El Pachon project and McEwen Mining’s 160,000t/y Los Azules copper project in San Juan.  Similarly to Pascua Lama, El Pachon is also located on the Chile-Argentine border, and is based in an area susceptible to glaciation.  Projects in this region are likely to be facing delays and capital increases due to the unclear legislation. 

Teck Resources has temporarily withdrawn its SEIA (Social and Environmental Impact Assessment) application for the US$5.6B Quebrada Blanca Phase 2 project in Chile.  The development, which was expected to be commissioned in 2016 prior to the announcement, will eventually replace the current SXEW operation.  The reason for the withdrawal of the SEIA application remains unclear. 

Violent protests continue against Newmont’s Conga copper-gold project in Peru.  It was reported in early July that 5 people had been killed during clashes with police and a state of emergency was declared.  In late June, Newmont announced that it would revise the project and remove two, not four, mountain lakes and replace them with reservoirs.  This work will be done in advance of the mine construction in a bid to reduce the local opposition to the project.  It is important to notice that the joint venture between Newmont and Buenaventura also runs the nearby Yanacocha mine, which has made several environmental and social mistakes over the past decade and this encourages mining opposition in the region.

Feelings among the residents are mixed, and although the majority approve the relocation, the company may yet experience opposition with residents refusing to move.

Smelting and electro-refining ###### 3.1 Overview After all adjustments and probabilities, we estimate that smelter production reached 3.40Mt of copper-in-blister in Q2 2012. This represents a 5.2% increase from Q1 2012, but only a 1.9% increase y-o-y. The main constraints on Q2 smelter production were constituted by maintenance shutdowns as well as technical problems. Further to the decline in demand for raw materials in Q2, the market for concentrates was also eased by better than expected mine supply, which increased from 2.97Mt of copper-inconcentrate in Q1 to 3.23Mt in Q2. As a result, we estimate that the deficit in raw materials supply had decreased from 155,000t in Q1 2012 to 35,000t in Q2. However, a dichotomy emerged between the supply of low and high quality concentrate, with increased demand for the latter putting downward pressure on TC/RCs on the spot market. Looking ahead, we expect the deficit in raw materials supply to re-intensify in Q2 as the smelter maintenance season comes to a close and as the PASAR smelter ramps up production, together with the recent commissioning of Yunnan Tin’s 100,000t/y smelter and the completion of the 50,000t/y expansion at Lihua International smelters, both in China.  Overall, we expect to see a raw materials deficit of 343,000t in 2012. 

Looking further afield, we have substantially revised our long term outlook on production and the raw materials balance following the suspension of environmental permits at several major smelting projects, including Sichuan Hongda’s 400,000t/y smelting project, Guangxi Nanguo Copper’s 150,000t/y smelting project and Qinghai Copper’s 100,000t/y smelting project, following public protests.  Additionally, the MIIT has announced the full list of smelting operations to be closed in 2012, which have a combined production capacity of 714,000t/y.  As a result, we have reduced our estimate for 2016 committed production from 19.14Mt to 18.59Mt, with the 2016 raw materials deficit revised down

We expect that by 2016, average smelters’ utilisation rates will rise to 72.3%, from 67.7% in 2012. ###### 3.2 Smelter production issues ###### **3.2.1 Smelting utilisation rates** Weak supply of raw materials (both in terms of quantity and quality) in conjunction with ever increasing smelting capacity is continually squeezing smelters’ utilisation rates. After all disruption allowances and raw materials availability adjustments, we estimate that 2012 smelter utilisation rates will average 67.7% globally. This is slightly up on our estimate of 67.3% in the April issue of this report. The change comes as a result of a fall in the raw materials deficit. This is in part due to our expectation of reduced smelter production as a result of technical failures, multiple maintenance shutdowns and uncertainties over China’s future copper demand. Additionally, better than expected mine production in Q2, especially with an uptick in concentrate output from the Escondida mine, has also helped ease the deficit. Interestingly, in spite of our reduction to committed smelter production this year, we now expect blister output to actually increase by 76,000t compared to our April forecast, as smelters are better able to secure adequate material in a less tight market. Furthermore, delays in start-ups and ramp-ups have also helped to ease the market, culminating in increased utilisation rates. The global average utilisation rate should, however, be treated with caution as smelting performance is highly geographically diverse. Canada is expected to see the highest utilisation rates for the second year running, which we estimate will average 83.7% this year. The boost to Canadian utilisation rates came since the closure of operations at Kidd Creek and Flin Flon in mid-2010, which reduced national smelting and refining capacity, leaving the rest of the smelters in a better position to obtain raw materials. Elsewhere in North America, the reopening of the Buenavista mine will benefit the La Caridad smelter in Mexico. However, smelters in the US continue to underperform and are expected to reach an average utilisation rate of just 67.7% this year. Our preliminary estimates indicate that production of copper-in-concentrate in Q2 reached 3.23Mt, up by 7.7% from Q1 2012, and up by 3.5% y-o-y. Overall, there were few immediate disruptions to production during the quarter, with only sporadic weather disruptions in South America and insubstantial strikes at various mines around the world, although concerns over output levels at Grasberg persisted into Q2. Meanwhile, there have been no reports of any significant infrastructure or technical problems and we expect that ore grades in Q2 remained stable, with Q1 grades up by 0.9% y-oy, based on a sample of 48 mines. From the perspective of copper concentrate grades, the average copper content of exported Chilean material has increased in the first two months of Q2 2012. Concentrate grades from the region averaged 30.0% during this period, compared with an average grade of 28.9% in Q1. The greatest improvements in concentrate grades were observed at Anglo American Sur’s operations, which saw a 5.3% rise from Q1, as well as at the Collahuasi mine, where the concentrate grades increased by 4.6% from Q1. Minera Escondida also saw a marked increase of 1%, reflecting the fact that the mine has overcome some of the low ore grade problems experienced in Q4 2011-Q1 2012. Concentrate grades at other mines in the region remained relatively flat, except for Anglo American Norte’s operations, where grades fell by 2.9%. However, we are still awaiting data from Codelco, whose concentrate grades are typically lower than average, which may deflate the quarterly average. Looking ahead, we expect copper-in-concentrate production to reach 12.6Mt in 2012, up by just 0.2% on last year’s total. However, new production set to come on stream from late 2012 should help lift output in 2013 by 7.2% to 13.5Mt after applying all probabilities and adjustments. We CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly July 2012 Chapter 2 67 anticipate a period of robust production to follow, with a compound annual growth rate of 6.8% between 2013 and 2016. By 2017, we expect world copper-in-concentrate output to reach 16.4Mt, up by 5.2Mt on the level in 2011. However, we do see more downside than upside risk to this forecast, as over the past six months we have been seeing growing obstacles to project development, causing many projects to be pushed back or even cancelled. In particular, resource nationalism has become

a key concern, with many governments hiking up taxes, limiting the repatriation or profits, controlling exports, demanding greater ownership stakes and applying stricter regulations. This is quickly becoming a key deterrent to mining investment, alongside rising development costs, an uncertain price outlook and faltering demand from China. Overall, we expect concentrate demand from smelters to increase proportionately faster than growth in concentrate supply until 2016, when the deficit is likely to begin to narrow. 

The spot market for concentrate has tightened from Q1, when reduced Chinese buying activity due to the unfavourable SHFE/LME arbitrage and the Spring Festival holiday, together with the unprecedented shutdowns at Pan Pacific Copper’s (PPC) Saganoseki and PASAR’s Leyte smelters boosted TC/RCs.  Although mine copper-in-concentrate production increased in Q2 and demand eased due to maintenance shutdowns and the closure of PASAR, the lack of scrap on the market and increased demand for clean concentrate for blending with more complex material, particularly concentrates containing arsenic, put downward pressure on TC/RCs.  Spot mine/trader TC/RCs in Q2 narrowed to 41.00/4.10 from 33.00/3.30 in Q1.  Meanwhile, average spot TC/RCs agreed in China narrowed from 45.00/4.50 in Q1 to 41.00/4.10 in Q2. We expect for spot TC/RCs to remain narrow in the short term following the re-commissioning of PASAR’s Leyte smelter in late June and the end of maintenance downtimes at numerous other smelters. 

###### **Scrap** 

The global scrap market tightened in Q2 2012.  This was predominantly attributed to poor supply caused by scrap merchants withholding material from the market as a result of the continuing fall in refined copper prices. The average LME cash copper price averaged US$7,869/t in Q2, down by US$441/t from Q1 2012.  Furthermore, refined copper prices fell consistently throughout the quarter, from an average US$8,260/t in April to US$7,421/t in June. As a consequence, scrap traders opted to limit supply, faced with the prospect of having to sell below cost until prices recovered.  Overall, scrap discounts narrowed significantly in all regions in Q2, with China experiencing the greatest fall. 

In addition to a fall in refined copper prices, the undersupply of scrap in China was constrained further by the negative arbitrage between the SHFE and the LME in combination with continuing growth in demand from smelters.  The arbitrage between the SHFE and the LME averaged US$-206 throughout Q2, severely constraining imports, which were down by 2.9% y- o-y to 1.16Mt.  As a result, discounts for imported No. 2 scrap averaged US$437/t in Q2, representing a narrowing of 19.5% from the previous quarter.  Meanwhile, the market for domestic scrap also tightened, with discounts of No.2 material narrowing by 15.0% in the same period to US$487/t.  The supply of domestic scrap has been further constrained by poor generation caused by a slowdown in IP and a

subdued construction sector. Although the tightness in the Chinese scrap market has been offset somewhat by slowing demand for scrap CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly July 2012 Chapter 2 68 from semi-fabricators, this easing mainly applies to No.1 scrap demand, which is favoured by this sector. Looking ahead, the prospects for Chinese copper scrap supply are set to improve, as the government’s recent monetary policy loosening, in conjunction with the introduction of numerous subsidies for consumers of end-use goods, should help boost refined copper prices, which should in turn encourage scrap merchants to return to the market. Furthermore, scrap generation is expected to improve on account of the government’s recent policies promoting the recycling of motor vehicles and the anticipated rise in home appliance recycling. The European scrap market tightened somewhat in Q2 as a result of material being withheld by scrap merchants in the light of low refined copper prices as well as due to poor generation. However, poor supply has, to an extent, been offset by lacklustre demand from Chinese buyers, who were constrained by the negative arbitrage, as well as through diminishing demand from European smelters in the latter part of the period, as activity began to wind down ahead of the summer holidays. Scrap generation in Europe has been subdued due to a slowdown in economic activity, however, a dichotomy emerged between the north and south of the continent. In southern Europe, generation has been particularly poor as a result of a struggling construction sector, whereas, scrap has been more readily available in northern nations due to a seasonal uptick in demolition activity. Nonetheless, this was offset to an extent by the recent bans on cash-payments for scrap in France and the Netherlands. Overall, discounts for No. 2 scrap in Europe narrowed by 14.6% in Q2 to US$440/t. Smelters have reported that a waiting game has ensued, with scrap users not desperate enough to buy at the current narrow discounts and scrap merchants reluctant to sell at the low copper prices. We expect activity in the European market to remain quiet until September, when business recovers from the holiday months. The scrap market in the US tightened the least of all the major scrap-using regions in Q2, with discounts narrowing just 3.5% from the prev

ious quarter. A rebound in the construction sector, in conjunction with an absence of Chinese buyers from the US scrap market, has meant that CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly July 2012 Chapter 2 69 scrap has been in steady supply despite the fall in refined copper prices. Nonetheless, the market tightened somewhat in May and June, which market insiders attributed to the commissioning of SDI La Farga’s wirerod plant in New Haven. The plant utilises No. 2 scrap to achieve production of approximately 80,000t/y of wirerod and has been buying up material ahead of beginning production throughout the quarter through its subsiduary OmniSource. ###### **4.2.3 Other disruptions** ###### **Technical issues** Following a six-month outage caused by a fire in January, PASAR’s Leyte smelter and refinery in the Philippines is being re-commissioned. According to market insiders, the smelter began heating up on 28th June, however, the electrostatic precipitator, which was severely damaged in January’s fire, requires further reconstruction work with two of its eight chambers yet to be completed. Full smelting and refining operations remain some weeks off and so full commercial production should restart no sooner that the end of July, and more likely in August. No estimates were given of the expected production losses from the six-month shutdown. The Leyte smelter has an annual capacity of 210,000t/y copper-in-blister, but typically produces 150,000t/y. While the six-month shutdown of the smelter constituted a major disruption, the impact of the outage on the refined market has been relatively muted. This was possible due to Glencore’s (78% owner of PASAR) role as a major trader in both the concentrates and refined copper markets, enabling the company to divert the incoming raw materials meant for the smelter to the spot market via its trading arm and also secure supplies of refined copper to cover its supply commitments. Nonetheless, we expect a tightening of the spot market for copper concentrate as increasing quantities of material are diverted back to the smelter. In other news, we have heard reports that Yunnan Tin’s recently commissioned copper smelter has encountered difficulties during ramp-up. The magnitude of these problems, however, CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly July 2012 Chapter 2 70 remains unclear as no official statement has been made by the company at the time of writing. ###### **Environmental/Government issues** 

The construction of Sichuan Hongda Molybdenum and Copper’s smelter and refinery project in China’s Sichuan province has been cancelled by the local government after local residents protested due to their concerns over the development’s environmental impact, despite the project having received environmental approval in March 2012.  The US$1.6B project was expected to produce 400,000t of copper cathode and 40,000t of molybdenum at full capacity. Earlier in the quarter, under similar circumstances, approvals of environmental impact assessments were suspended for Guangxi Nanguo Copper’s 150,000t/y copper smelting project by the Ministry of Environmental Protection (MEP). These developments highlight shifting attitudes towards heavy industry within China due to increasing environmental awareness.  The Chinese authorities have initiated closures of outdated smelting capacity due to energy inefficiency and pollution many times in recent years, but these are the first incidents where the construction of a new, technologically advanced and efficient copper plants have been halted due to local opposition. Community action is often a major disruptive factor in other parts of the world, but this is a new development in China.  Considering the country’s huge and expanding smelting/refining sector, further activism in this area could have a substantial impact on the copper market balance. 

In other environmental developments, Dundee Precious Metals’ Tsumeb complex was recently ordered by the Namibian authorities to reduce feed input by half, citing environmental concerns. However, in mid-July the order was revoked after the smelter received a clean bill of heal

th from the Department of Environment and Tourism.  The smelter treats arsenic-bearing concentrates from Dundee’s Chelopech mine in Bulgaria.  Had the order been enforced, concentrates from Chelopech would have been difficult to redistribute to other smelters, as none have the facilities to treat the arsenic-rich material and it would need to be blended with clean material. 

Lastly, Doe Run Peru, the owner of the 75,000t/y La Oroya smelter in Peru, has gone into liquidation after the company’s shareholders rejected a restructuring plan proposed in April

###### **4.2.4 The sulphuric acid market** 

The sulphuric acid market started out fairly quietly in Q2, but began to progressively tighten in the second half of the quarter. In April, suppliers in both Europe and the US reported good quantities of acid available to the market, while Asian markets remained quiet. Demand from China was muted as the end of the ploughing season in the north of the country reduced the consumption of fertilisers and demand from the industrial sector has not been able to fully compensate for this. Chilean spot prices in April were quoted in the range of US$70-90/t CFR Mejillones. The calmness continued into the beginning of May across all regions, but shortly after, the market tightened as many smelters embarked on scheduled maintenance. In particular, supply tightened in Europe, the Mediterranean and the Americas, and by the end of May prices rose, albeit offset somewhat by concerns about the Eurozone. By June, the sulphuric acid market tightened in all regions with spot prices in Europe and Asia following those in the Americas upwards on reduced supply and strong demand. By the end of the month, Chilean spot prices were reaching upwards of US$130/t CFR Mejillones. This is understood to be due to a shortfall in local supply as a result of the delays to the restart of the Noracid plant earlier in the year combined with technical problems and the scheduled 55-day maintenance at Codelco’s Chuquicamata smelter. There was, however, reported to be resistance from buyers at these prices. 

As discussed earlier, a number of copper smelters have recently had, are undergoing, or are about to begin maintenance downtime, reducing acid availability in a number of regions. Most affected was the Asian region with two major smelters, Yanggu Xianggu

ang and Jinlong, out in China in May/June as well as the Gresik smelter in Indonesia in May. However, the biggest single loss will be in Chile, due to the upcoming maintenance closure at Chuquicamata. The smelter normally produces over 1Mt/y of acid. However, the re-start of PASAR’s Leyte plant is set to ease the market. By early July, the first Q3 contract prices had been agreed in Europe at rollover or with a small increase on Q2 levels, averaging €70-80/t, despite rising spot prices. At the end of Q2, the market was finely balanced, but strong demand from DAP producers in North Africa was affecting sentiment. This in turn boosted spot prices in the Americas, particularly Brazil and Chile. The trader that secured a 60,000t tender from Boliden was looking to achieve a delivered price of $115/t into Brazil, and other traders were reported to be offering material for prices of well over the $100/t mark.
