The most active participant in the spot market in recent weeks has been Codelco, which over

the last three months has placed a total of 170,000t of concentrates. Technical problems and a planned 55-day maintenance closure at its Chuquicamata smelter as well as a reduced level of output at Ventanas has left the company with spare material. The company’s internal concentrate balance has increased in any case with the start up of concentrate output at Radomiro Tomic at the end of 2010. Some of the material offered by Codelco has, however, been from its Chuquicamata mine with elevated arsenic levels. We also heard that Glencore offered concentrates displaced by the closure of Leyte into the Chinese market, but the recent re-start of this smelter means that this material is no longer available. The continued closure of La Oroya in Peru means that there are increasing tonnages of complex material seeking a home. This material can only be placed by blending, placing increased pressure on the market for clean concentrates. Demand for spot concentrates from the Chinese smelters has been subdued over the last quarter, reflecting the negative SHFE/LME arbitrage and weak demand for copper cathode. Recent trends ###### Prices sink below $8,000/t from mid-May While macroeconomic data in the first few months of the year remained generally gloomy, the copper price rebounded solidly above $8,000/t as a result of strong Chinese import data at the turn of the year and confirmation of weaker production in 2011 as annual reports came in. However, in early April the price retreated due to persistent worries over the global economy and Chinese demand. Meanwhile, the US outlook cooled on lower than expected jobs growth data and indications given out by the Federal Reserve that another stimulus package would not be introduced soon, contrary to the expectations of many. Further downward pressure was applied to the price by the increasing apprehension in the market over Chinese demand growth prospects for 2012. From mid-April the price rebounded as market players attending CESCO week found themselves in broad agreement over a resurgence of Chinese demand in H2, while weaker preliminary Q1 supply data bolstered support. The simultaneous warrant cancellations on 20th April, discussed later on in this section, squeezed near-term availability outside China during t

he following week. With open interest falling at the same time, it appeared that the squeeze had precipitated a round of short covering, which kick-started a resurgence in the price. Prices pushed lower throughout May, falling below $8,000/t from the middle of the month and continuing to descend, reaching below $7,400/t by 1st June. As the accompanying chart indicates, this declining trend was in line with movements in the US dollar and the general global economic picture. Gloom over the world’s financial health intensified in May, as fears in Europe began to turn to the potential for Greece to leave the Eurozone and, more recently, the CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly July 2012 Chapter 3 85 threat from defaulting Spanish banks opening another chapter in the saga of the single currency. The unwinding of the backwardation also caused a sharper drop for LME cash prices. In early June, the price then tested downside support and found it, with the 3-month price hitting an intra-day traded low of $7,270/t on 8th June. Given the high level of uncertainty, prices then traded sideways ahead of the Greek election on 17th June. In the event, the results of the Greek election were as positive as could be expected with the probailout party winning a narrow majority, and so the copper price rallied to over $7,600/t on 19th June. However, the internal contradictions of the Eurozone prompted bond markets to turn on Spain and Italy, driving bond yields for their sovereign debt towards the crisis levels of 7%. In response, investors fled back to safe havens and the copper price fell back to test the recent downside support level, which held again. The next turn of the short term price cycle came after the results of the Eurozone summit on 28th June, which boosted sentiment among financial investors. The strict stance of German Chancellor Angela Merkel against bailing out struggling banks was softened. Among the measures taken, the European Stability Mechanism was allowed to directly recapitalise banks with its debt having the same level of seniority as existing loans in the event of bankruptcy. As a result,

febrile sentiment switched rapidly into "risk on" mode, with the 3-month price on the LME jumping to a trading high of $7,819/t on 3rd July. In the next fortnight, prices held in the range of $7,500-7,800/t. ###### Low stocks outside China push LME backwardation.... Possibly the most interesting trend which emerged in the last quarter was the sustained and deep backwardation position seen between LME cash and 3-month prices. It began when the depletion of warehouse stocks outside China created severe tightness in the market in late March, and moving into April, the near-term scarcity in the US and Europe was keenly felt. Investors needing to cover short positions found themselves struggling to source material, which lent support to cash prices. Another driver was that many copper consumers had overbooked supplies of copper cathode in 2011, having had higher expectations of demand than what actually turned out to be the case. This meant that in 2012 the consumers opted to be more cautious, but as demand has been a little better than many feared, these same consumers need to keep coming back to the spot market for material. In this environment, falling stock levels in the LME warehouses meant that material available for prompt delivery was valued higher than 3-month copper. As a result, having been in contango for over a year, LME copper cash and 3-month prices moved into backwardation in mid-March and remained there in early-to-mid-April. As the following chart indicates, the record level of total LME warrant cancellations on 20th April caused a steep drop in open tonnages around the world, sparking a reinvigorated dive into backwardation as those short on the LME were caught out by the sudden reduction in available stock in the LME system and had to bid up nearby prices to cover their positions. This culminated in the back reaching over -$152/t by the end of the month - the largest one-day backwardation value seen since August 2008 and the deepest sustained move into backwardation since mid-2008. This record level of warrant cancellations occurred around the world, with 6 LME warehouses registering an atypically high level of cancellations on the same day. The USA, Europe and Asia all saw open tonnages decline that day, leading some to suspect a coordinated move. The CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly July 2012 Chapter 3 86 market rumours were that the cancellation was the work of one large trader who was squeezing short positions held mainly by Chinese smelters, several of which made an announcement that they would make a concerted effort to deliver metal to the LME to help rebalance the market. While CRU refrains from pointing any fingers, we acknowledge that there are a (small) number of trading houses which certainly have the capability to arrange such a move. As the market imbalance between stocks within and without China became more obvious, there was scope for Chinese cathode exporters to make a profit and so material began to move into LME Asia warehouses. The differential was very volatile in the first half of May, with backwardation values ranging from $25/t to over $142/t. However, in the second half of the month there was a shift as more metal was delivered into LME warehouses and the differential narrowed to around $40/t from just over $100/t in the first half of the month. LME Asia open tonnages have continued to build, influencing further narrowing of the differential and a move back into contango territory in mid-June. However, the tightness between dates behind the move into backwardation never really fully cleared. Instead of moving into a smooth contango structure (with the price for each forward date higher than the previous one) in June the kink in the curve shifted out a few months to the September contract. The LME warrant banding report also showed that a dominant warrant holder had arrived, with one player holding 40-50% of the stocks in LME warehouses in June, but that this fell to 30-40% as of 3rd July. ###### ...while China’s stock build eases, then reverses The Chinese stock build which began in December 2011 finally started to subside in April/May, and CRU estimates that by the end of June bonded warehouse stocks declined substantially to around 500,000t, from a high of about 650,000 in mid-May. In total, SHFE and bonded warehouse stocks are estimated to have increased from around 265,000t at the end of November last year to a peak of roughly 805,000t at the end of April 2012. Nevertheless, it became apparent at the start of Q2 that the build-up was decelerating, as consumption began to pick up and imports decreased from March. Additionally, the negative SHFE/LME arbitrage was providing opportunities for traders to re-export material from China. At the end of April, a number of Chinese smelters including Jiangxi Copper announced a joint agreement to deliver cathode to the LME over the next two months, ostensibly to ease tightness in the global market. Refined exports increased to around 27,000t in March and April, from only 700t in February. However, the real jump in exports came in May, at a record amount of over 102,000t, reflecting the involvement of the copper smelters. In the corresponding period, the LME’s Asian warehouses recorded tonnages increasing from 35,250t to 70,000t at the end of May. Most of the rise has been in the South Korean warehouses that are nearest to China. The total LME Asia tonnage grew to 111,150t by the end of June, confirming our understanding that exports have continued out of China. However, the copper smelters in China who had exported in May announced that they had stopped exporting in early June. The strong growth in LME Asian warehouses did slow throughout the second half of June, indicating that this is likely to have been the case. CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly July 2012 Chapter 3 88 ###### Mines and projects get more attention from stakeholders The first six months of 2012 have certainly seen lower levels of mine disruption than in the previous year, and fairly low levels of disruption relative to other years as well. In particular, the volume of lost production due to strike action and labour-related disruption is much lower. Ore grades have been lower in many mines, but at Escondida there has been a big recovery in grades in H1 due to the Escondida Ore Access Project, resulting in an increase in copper-inconcentrate production of 24.0% for the first half, y-o-y. Overall, Q2 primary copper production is estimated at 4.14Mt of contained copper, which is a 3.4% increase on the same quarter last year. On the downside, however, there have been a number of incidences in H1 of stakeholders taking action that could disrupt operations or projects and possibly deter investment. We can broadly split stakeholder disruption into two main categories: - **Governmental disruption.** This typically inv

olves so-called “resource nationalism”, whereby governments aim to increase revenues from operations or insist on domestic raw materials processing. - **Local community disruption.** This typically flares up over perceptions of risk to the environment, community health and/or water supplies, leading to protest action from local communities over environmental or social issues. Examining governmental disruption and resource nationalism first of all, this is a trend which has intensified during the commodities super-cycle. Governments and their electorates have, of course, noticed the boom in metals prices in the last decade, and the perception of the revenues of mining companies often leads to the conclusion that the national or local share of profits is too low. As the chart below indicates, typical major changes to government mining codes or policies involve raising royalties or blocking the export of raw materials (either by an outright ban or via prohibitive taxation). Besides the trend for increasing resource taxes, there is also widespread enthusiasm amongst the governments of the developing world for the idea of bringing downstream processing into their countries to gain further value share and jobs. The prevail

ing view is that since the mineral resources of a country, once mined, can only be processed and sold once, so it should be done domestically at optimal revenue and benefit to the country.  However, the truth of the copper market is that smelting and refining will only provide the last 10% or so of value, and with a global raw materials deficit set to continue beyond the refined deficit (primarily due to continuing Chinese smelter capacity expansions) the world is more in need of copper concentrate exporting mines than new copper smelters. 

Local community disruptions have much broader motivations.  They may also be motivated by money or enhancements to local services (schools, hospitals etc), but just as frequently, if not more so, their main concern is preserving their current quality of life.  Apprehensions tend to centre on access to clean water, environmental protection, and sudden social changes.  Peru is arguably the country with the greatest challenge in this regard for mine operations and development.  However, recently the Chilean government has drafted a legal framework around the ILO-convention 169, which gives certain rights to indigenous populations regarding the use of their land.  The proposed framework bears some similarities to that already in place in Peru, and could potentially bring some of the same problems in Peru to Chile. 

In the Philippines, while the government has recently completed its review of mining law and recommended higher taxes, it has also begun steps to lift the moratorium on new mining applications with an executive order issued by Philippines’ president Benigno Aquino III on July 9<sup>th</sup> requiring local mining regulation to be consistent with national laws.  This is good news for the Tampakan project, where development work has been held up since January when the project was refused an environmental permit by the local government due to a ban on open-pit mining in the South Cotabato province it is situated in.  However, this project is facing fierce opposition from NGOs, the Catholic Church and local communities, whose lobbying had caused the ban on open pit mining to be created in the first place.  These groups are opposed on the grounds of environmental damage with the removal of areas of rainforest, potential pollution and changes to the way of life of locals. 

These issues mostly affect projects and therefore the medium term view of where the copper market is heading.  However, the medium term view affects the short term view through the influence of hedge fund investment that “brings forward” the fundamentals, as we discuss in the next section.

###### Despite lower H2 imports, China to log a surplus in 2012… 

As noted at the end of the previous section, mine projects are the main driver of the production side of the copper market equation.  However, the wave of new p

rojects will not begin to strongly boost refined production until 2013. The other significant influence on prices is the behaviour of investors. These players have been suffering from the continuing dislocations in the financial markets, which are not about to end and will continue to promote high levels of price volatility. We forecast that global refined consumption growth will be 3.5% this year. Matching this up with our forecast of flat refined growth leaves the refined market in deficit by almost 480,000t. As our new Table 3.4 on page ?? shows, this deficit accrues in the World ex-China where we forecast a shortfall in cathode of over 600,000t. Almost 500,000t of this comes from a drawdown in unreported stocks, which mostly happened in Q1. Chinese import data shows that the increase in refined imports by China has come from all the countries with major refined producers. This suggests that the unreported stocks probably came from producers taking advantage of the high prices and uncertainty over the demand outlook to ship as much metal as possible. High Chinese refined imports in H1 will not be fully offset by our forecast of a reduction in imports in H2 this year. As a result, we anticipate that the Chinese market will be in surplus by 126,000t for 2012 as a whole. …helping to keep the price in check for the rest of the year Despite the large deficit, the LME price has been subdued over the past couple of months and we forecast it will average around $7,500/t ($3.40/lb) in Q3. As far as the fundamentals are concerned, a global deficit in the quarter will not draw down stocks much, as most of this is forecast to be supplied from a decline of inventory in China. In addition, the uncertainty over the Eurozone crisis will keep investors on the sidelines. Medium term outlook ###### Supply surge to bring prices down We now forecast that 45 new mine operations will start up in 2014, however there have been some probable and possible projects pushed further out. In total, these additions plus the continued ramp up of projects that had started up in 2012 and 2013 will lift refined production growth 4.3% in 2014. Production from new mine projects will be fed by 49 start-ups in 2015 and 37 in 2016. Total potential production in 2016 from new projects starting up during 2012-2016 is 8.8Mt. ###### Key risks to the price outlook In 2012, risks to the price around the base case are fairly balanced, as the range forecast in the chart above demonstrates. The range is wider than in previous quarterlies, as we have widened the bands to better reflect historical copper price ranges. Downside macroeconomic and financial risks and their consequent negative impact on consumption are offsetting the upside risks of lower copper production and higher investor inflows into copper. One point to note is that Chinese buying as the price falls below $7,000/t provides a floor for the price. In 2013, as the forecast is lower than in April, the risks remain symmetrical. From 2014 to 2016, the risks become biased to the high side, as production risks come to the fore, driven principally by production possibly underperforming compared to the base case. The downside risks come from demand significantly underperforming the base through some form of intensified economic disruptions, most likely driven by another financial sector shock. ###### Production risks Production risks to the price are mostly to the upside. The first is that tight availability of equipment, qualified personnel, water, power, etc. mean that sequencing of projects (at both the company and industry levels) will be a serious challenge. The second is the increasing level of challenges to projects (mine and smelter/refinery) from government and community relations as discussed in the Recent Trends section. Consequently, we believe that there is a greater downside than upside risk to our production forecast and therefore an upward bias to the price forecast, especially in the 2014-16 period, when there is significant risk that mine projects will not come on as expected in the base case. There is some downside risk from production. We have a mine disruption allowance in the 20142016 period of 12-13% and have made allowances for project risks of a 10% underperformance for firm projects, 30% for probable and 60% for possible ones. If our macroeconomic forecast turns out to be too optimistic, then demand could be less and the wave of mine projects could come on just in time to swamp the market and drive down prices sooner than in our base case. CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly July 2012 Chapter 3 98 ###### Macroeconomic and financial risks The key risk to the copper price is the uncertainty of how the global economy will perform. The apparent improvement in the US could prove short-lived and China could possibly not see a return to growth in H2 2012. The Eurozone crisis could also still prompt more financial market turmoil. The safe haven status of the US dollar in a crisis could also see it strengthen faster than we have accounted for in the base case, which would be negative for a dollar denominated price. On the other hand, in the near term the continuing

tightness in the forward curve shows that another squeeze could be engineered. The resulting move into backwardation at the front end of the forward curve could lead to a higher price outturn than in our base case. In addition, economic growth in both the US and China could prove stronger than forecast in the base case. This would be positive for growth in these important consuming countries, but also in those emerging markets which export to these two large economies. It would also provide a spur to investors to boost holdings of risk assets such as copper. ###### Consumption risks ###### Downside Aluminium producers are currently facing challenging conditions, with the industry in a situation of chronic oversupply. Smelter closures began in the beginning of 2012, with many of the closures directly impacting captive hot metal wirerod plants at aluminium smelters. So, despite a Cu:Al price ratio of almost 4:1, supply constraints are likely to prevent aluminium from increasing its market share in the rod sector in the short term. Longer term though, the substitution threat remains significant for copper demand growth in wirerod. We expect aluminium will make more inroads into the insulated power cable market as a result of an increase in aluminium wirerod capacity available to target this segment by 2015. CRU forecasts that the ratio of the copper price to that of aluminium will average close to 4:1, which will weigh on all consumers’ strategic decision-making regarding substituting away from copper. ###### Upside The potential shortage of scrap for direct use (due to weaker generation) could lead to additional cathode requirements, especially in China. A double-dip recession would only accelerate the emerging markets decoupling their economic growth further from the industrialised countries by favouring copper-intensive domestic demand. Some Chinese consumers or the SRB could see copper as a bargain for speculative purposes at prices much lower than our base case, thus leading to higher cathode imports. As a result of RMB appreciation, further support for copper could also emerge from a diversion of surplus cash away from the dollar and directly into commodity investments as a means of diversification. ###### 5.1 LME price movements 

Over the last three months, investor activity in the LME metals markets has been dominated, primarily, by events in Europe.  The chart below plots the US dollar/euro exchange rate against the series which is the total US dollar value of one contract of each of the six LME metals.  The close relationship between the two over this timeframe is clearly evident from the chart. Moreover, from an anecdotal perspective, good news regarding policy or economic performance from either the US or China had very little effect on investors’ willingness to invest in commodities. 

Metal prices rallied slightly after the Fed’s FOMC statement on April 25<sup>th</sup> which indicated that the US economy was showing better than expected improvement.  However, LME prices began a month-long slide after elections on May 6<sup>th</sup> installed Socialist Franзois Hollande as the President of France, and the major anti-austerity party in Greece was asked to form a government.  As of May 17<sup>th</sup> , Greece’s political parties were unable to come to a power-sharing arrangement, so parliament was dissolved and new elections were scheduled for June 17<sup>th</sup> .  This lack of political leadership increased the speed of capital flight from Greece’s banks, causing many to question whether Greece would stay in the Eurozone, or whether the Eurozone would survive at all.  Not surprisingly, the euro lost ground to the US dollar, and metal prices followed suit. 

In early June, the “sell in May and go away” adage appeared to have run its course.  LME metals shrugged off news of a downgrade to Spain’s sovereign credit rating and the subsequent announcement that Spain would apply to the EU for bank bailout funds.  Metals were relatively steady ahead of Greece’s elections on June 17<sup>th</sup> , in which the pro-bailout party was victorious, as well as the Fed’s FOMC regular 2-day meeting on June 19<sup>th</sup> and 20<sup>th</sup> .

For Q3 2012, we expect an average of $1.25/€ (€0.80/$) and, as we write on 13th July, the euro is trading slightly weaker at $1.225/€ (€0.816/$). This perfectly illustrates the problem that investors are facing with regard to choosing to allocate money to commodities. Even though the Chinese economy will improve during the next six to nine months, which means that commodity demand is likely to gather momentum, the outlook points to a stronger US dollar during that timeframe. In fact, in the very short term, the uncertainty around the euro is so high that it is not clear how far it might decline before it finally stabilizes. Thus, potentially, any price gains in commodities that might occur due to stronger physical market fundamentals could be eliminated completely by a stronger US dollar. This explains why commodity market investors remain on the sidelines, preferring to hold cash. The comparative analysis of asset classes in Q2 2012 indicates that equities and bonds are not performing terribly well, either, so money isn’t moving from commodities to other places; rather, it’s waiting to find its next destination. We have written before that the “commodity story” for investors had two pillars. The first was a trend toward a weaker US dollar over the long-term. The second was the likelihood that emerging markets, particularly China, would need more metal to fuel their development. CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly July 2012 Chapter 3 106 In terms of the US dollar, the near term picture is extremely cloudy. The EU has made some concrete, and well-received, decisions to create and implement a

n infrastructure which will insulate member governments from the danger of failing banks.  However, this is still a promise, and not yet a fact.  Moreover, having an infrastructure to handle these issues does not eliminate the negative impact that more bank failures will have on the region’s economy. 

Economic growth in the US is unlikely to be given much additional support in terms of either central bank or government stimulus between now and the end of this year.  The United States is facing a Presidential campaign, which will be contentious, and Congressional elections will be no different.  However, the next US fiscal year ends begins in October so the sitting Congress will have to find a way to avoid the automatic tax increases and spending cuts which will occur, by law, in January 2013 – the proverbial “fiscal cliff”.  Note that all 435 members of the House of Representatives and 33 of the 100 Senators will be up for election in November as well.  Since the House has primary responsibility for formulating the budget, it is in the interest of every member of Congress to find a way to avoid upsetting the majority of the US electorate. 

In China, inflation remains below the central bank’s target.  Benchmark deposit rates and lending rates have already been reduced and the June data on bank lending show that it has increased relative to May.  Bank reserve ratios have been cut so the message is clear – Beijing wants to see more economic growth.  However, the current low level of price inflation indicates that domestic demand is still rather lacklustre, so policymakers are probably not yet finished with their stimulus programme. 

All of this, however, is a sideshow compared to what Europe does to manage its twin banking and sovereign debt crises.  This is the biggest concern for all market participants, commercial and speculative alike, so the prices will continue to be very headline-driven and react very quickly to developments in Europe.  Volatility is not the ideal environment to encourage a longer-term commitment from commodity investors.  Instead, they will look for a clear sign of stability in the euro before having the confidence to commit their capital to the commodity sector in a significant way.

# Appendix A: Industrial and economic outlook, 2012-2016 

###### 1. Eurozone malaise takes a further toll 

The **rerun of the Greek election on 17 June** changed surprisingly little.  It probably did no more than delay Greece’s slow descent into effective default.  Meanwhile the **malaise is spreading** , to Spain, and even to Germany.  As a result our Eurozone forecasts remain well below the consensus.  Maintaining our bearish stance we’ve **downgraded several of our emerging market forecasts** , because of first quarter growth in the cases of Brazil and India, and second quarter indicators in China.  Elsewhere we’ve trimmed modestly to reflect the **debil

itating effects of the uncertainty** surrounding the Eurozone, which is holding back production plans, investment and hiring at firms globally. 

**Worryingly, the outlook is as clouded as ever by downside risk.** Thus the **shortcomings of the plan to recapitalise Spain’s banks** highlights a greater threat than that of political failure in Greece, because it tells us that **contagion is already at work** .  The real concern is that events are moving beyond the reach of policy makers. Our **downside scenario** , to which we attach a probability close to 50%,  assumes that the Eurozone’s defences are soon overrun, leading to the **chaotic exit of several members, and a crunching recession** . 

- **Eurozone-driven uncertainty,** compounded by the approaching **‘fiscal cliff’** , is sapping corporate confidence in the USA, which in turn is inhibiting hiring and investment, and undermining what little confidence households have.  We see this remaining a drag on US growth through 2013 and beyond. 

- Early in June **Spain conceded that its financial sector was in deep crisis and applied for support** .  Almost inevitably the subsequent promise of €100 bn of funding was sufficiently vague that Spain’s borrowing costs rose to unsustainable rates anyway.   The **Eurozone** – half of which is already in recession – appears **locked into a cycle of muddling through at the cost of relentless austerity compounded by unrelenting uncertainty** . 

- **Neither is Asia immune from the Eurozone malaise. Japan** has just recorded its **first ever Eurozone deficit** .  Weaker shipments to the Eurozone are compounding the effects of the policy-induced slowdown in China.  Growth prospects are suffering as a result.  What’s more the downside risk for China, from the Eurozone, and too little too late policy-wise, is fostering concerns that the soft landing could harden up.

###### 2. Regional developments 

###### 2.1 The Americas: USA suffers summer doldrums again 

**The indications are that the USA is experiencing its third bout of summer softness in a row.** In recent weeks **first quarter GDP growth** was revised down from 2.2% annualised to **1.9%** , thanks to changes in the estimates of the contributions made by trade, stocks and public spending.   High frequency data suggests that the **second quarter’s performance won’t be much different** .  We have it at 2.2% annualised, but **the risks are that it could come in around 20 basis points lower.  For an economy which should be able to grow by 2.5% on trend, and somewhat above that during the recovery phase of its cycle, this is soft.** 

Last year the key problem was the dampening effects on spending caused by high oil prices. **This year the problem is mainly to do with the Eurozone’s downswing, and with the debilitating effects of the uncertainty emanating from the Eurozone on confidence.** One positive consequence is that inflation is falling back, which should support real spending in the second half of 2012.  As a result we’ve only shaved 10 basis points off our growth forecast for this year, trimming it to 2.2%.  The strong affinity to muddling through shown by policy makers in the Eurozone leads us to think that uncertainty will remain a dominant feature of the outlook for some time yet,  however, and the dampening effect this will have on confidence has led us to trim 10-20 basis points off our US growth forecasts through to 2016 as well. 

**The evidence of deceleration is widespread.** Industrial production eased down by 0.1% m- o-m in May, led by a broad-based 0.4% drop in manufacturing output.  In part this was payback for the unusual strength of production in the first quarter.  But on trend manufacturing has decelerated from double digit growth in the New Year to low single-digit growth now.  Further deceleration is likely: bookings for factory goods dropped in April, by 0.6% m-o-m for the third time in four months. 

**The USA’s dividend from rebalancing towards its external sector is diminishing as the crisis in the Eurozone intensifies.** This isn’t because of a serious loss of competitiveness, which is still high, although it’s being eroded at the margins by the weakening €,

but because of sharp absolute falls in demand and heightened uncertainty.   In April the 0.8% m-o-m fall back in exports was concentrated in capital goods and industrial supplies and materials.  The main weak spot in the USA’s markets was Europe, where demand for American goods has slumped dramatically on an annualised basis, from almost 15% growth in August 2011 to a contraction of almost 5% in April.  In contrast exports to China are still rising. 

**The slump in output is reflected in the labour market.** In May payrolls expanded at a very subdued rate for the third month in a row.  The increase was revised down from 115,000 in April to 77,000.  May hirings only increased by a net 69,000, which edged the unemployment rate back up to 8.2%.  Since then jobless claims have continued to trend gently upwards from the lows they hit in February and March.  The payback from the mild winter should have run its course by now, **so the deceleration in job creation points to underlying issues in the corporate sector** . 

Anecdotal evidence, plus surveys of corporate entities, indicates that the **perception that policy making in the Eurozone is stymied** , and the resultant uncertainty that belief fosters, exacerbated by **worries about the approaching fiscal cliff at home** , which we discussed last

One of the reasons the **US economy retains a degree of buoyancy,** which the Eurozone can only dream of, is that **policy remains supportive** .  On the fiscal front that will change early in 2013, but monetary policy is set to stay accommodating well beyond then.  The Federal Reserve’s (Fed’s) main policy rate is due to stay very low until late 2014.  But there’s more: in June the Fed launched a **further phase of Operation Twist** , whereby it sells short dated Treasury bills out to a maturity of three years and buys long-dated bills of a maturity of six years or more with the proceeds, thereby bearing down on long term yields and interest rates, but without expanding its balance sheet.  This operation could continue for another 3-4 months at present rates.  Beyond that, the Fed has a further round of **quantitative easing** (QE) **in reserve** , especially if the Eurozone’s dominos start to fall. 

In summary, the US economy is on a low growth trajectory to be sure, but barring a selfinflicted fiscal wound, we can be fairly confident it will continue to grow at least moderately. 

**Despite a raft of stimulus and protectionist measures, economic growth in Brazil has been much weaker than expected in the first half of 2012.** Brazil has achieved some success in stimulating job, income and credit growth through these policies but this has largely been through short-term incentives to consumption rather than structural policies aimed at improving investment.

###### 2.2 Europe: Spain takes centre stage 

An **imminent Greek exit from the Eurozone has been averted** following the relatively positive outcome of the Greek elections in early June.  However, the **new coalition that has been formed will find it difficult to negotiate a myriad of issues** , ranging from its own internal differences, to a strong opposition, and an increasingly impatient population suffering under the weight of a crippled economy.  This means a disorderly **Greek default is still likely to happen, and remains our base case** .  However, we also assume policymakers will do enough to avoid the worst of the contagion effects following this event.  Meanwhile, latest news of a **Spanish banking bail-out** is unlikely to make a material difference, and this view is echoed by financial markets which are still **demanding high yields on Spanish** (and Italian) debt.  In this climate of uncertainty, the **real economy is showing signs of contraction in the second quarter** of this year, with confidence effects now starting to impact on previously robust Germany.

###### 2.3 Asia: forecasts trimmed after first quarter data 

**Since the rude awakening provided by the release of April’s data there have been signs that China’s economy is beginning to take a turn for the better, driven by government policy.** Infrastructure investment is again being relied upon by the authorities to support growth, with rail, power and water projects to the fore.  Meanwhile, some targeted easing of house purchase restrictions plus improving affordability have seen housing sales strengthen since the start of May.  These developments are likely to be too little, too late as far as the second quarter is concerned, particularly for industrial production; we now expect GDP to grow by 7.7% year-on-year in the current quarter, with industrial production expanding by 9.7%. **Our full year GDP forecast is marked down from 8.2% to 8.0% and that for industrial production from 11.8% to 11.4% as a result.** 

**The government has been easing policy since the spring but has accelerated the process since early May when it became apparent that the economy was undershooting expectations.** Subsidies for purchases of energy efficient appliances, light bulbs and cars have been extended.  More significantly, investment projects in the Five Year Plan are being brought forward, particularly infrastructure investment in Central and Western China, and banks are being asked to lend to local governments.  The utilities sector is seeing strong investment across the board with an increase of 19.4% this year, the fastest rate of growth since the end of 2009. **By our calculations infrastructure Fixed Asset Investment (FAI) increased by nearly 5% y-o-y in real terms in May, which was a sharp turnaround from the 7% decline recorded in the second half of last year.**

erest rates,** to a one year lending rate of 6.31%, and a one year deposit rate of 3.25%. **This sent a strong signal that the government is serious about supporting the economy.** But more than that, the banks were given greater leeway to vary rates around the benchmarks.  On the lending side they are now allowed to charge as low as 0.8 times the benchmark rate, compared to 0.9 times previously.  On the deposit side banks can now offer up to 1.1 times the benchmark deposit rate having not had flexibility previously. **These**

###### 3. Alternative scenarios: Eurozone crashes 

**The result

of the Greek election** on 17 June reduced the risk of an imminent and chaotic Greek default, but it **didn’t alter the fundamentally impossible budgetary arithmetic facing Greece** .  Nor did it diminish the risks associated with Spain and Italy.   Each major bond redemption, each significant bank downgrade, poses the risk of a rapid descent into an unstoppable chain of crises, which could fast overtake policy making.  Thus **there remains a high probability that Greece will leave the Eurozone in the course of the coming quarters** . What’s more Spain’s deteriorating finances could make its position untenable, ahead, even, of Greece.  These are material risks, and either would likely trigger off a **domino effect** , leading to a series of exits.  Thus the abrupt departure of Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain and Italy from the Eurozone is the focus of this scenario.  For convenience we **assume that it begins in the third quarter of 2012** . 

What might a Eurozone crash look like?  The restored local **currencies** of the exiting countries would **depreciate sharply** , we assume by 50% against the euro in Greece, by 25% in Italy, Spain and Portugal, and by 15% in Ireland.  There would be **extensive collateral damage to asset prices** .  Thus equity prices could fall by 30% initially in Greece and remain 10% below base case levels through to the end of 2016.  In the other exiting countries equities might fall by 20% at the onset of the crisis and still be 8% below our base by the end of our forecast period. Elsewhere in the bloc equities could fall by 15% initially, but subsequently recover as the stronger northern Eurozone economies returned to growth. 

**The damage wouldn’t be limited to Europe, however.** We assume that stock markets would fall around 10% initially in the other major economies, but recover to base case values by 2016.  Meanwhile the banking sectors in the exiting countries and in the surviving rump of the Eurozone would suffer heavy losses and tighten credit standards dramatically.  These losses would imply the socialisation of significant additional debt.  As a result spreads on government bonds would rise by 1,200 bp in Greece and 1,100 bp in Portugal, Italy and Spain in the early stages of the crisis.  Business and consumer confidence would deteriorate sharply. 

**The euro might initially depreciate against the $ by 15%.** As the surviving rump of the Eurozone stabilised, the euro would begin appreciating, because of the inherent structural strength of the northern European economies, and it could end up end up around 15% stronger against the US dollar.   As a result the ECB would be likely to cut its policy rate to zero and keep it there until mid 2016.  A number of economies have signalled already that their monetary authorities would implement stimulus measures on a substantial scale in this event. 

In this scenario the **Eurozone would experience a recession in 2013 as severe as the downturn in 2009** , with the d

ifference that GDP would continue contracting in 2014. The exiting members would suffer crunching contractions, but Germany would succumb as well because of its trade links, and the collateral damage to its banks. The Eurozone would tip into deflation. The other developed economies would endure a downswing as well, and Chinese growth would fall below the target in its new Five Year plan, to the sort of rate at which the economy is unable to absorb all new entrants to the labour force. **Thus the global economy as a whole would contract in 2013, and world industrial output could fall by 5-6% that year.** CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly July 2012 Appendix A 121 |**Eurozone Downside**

set the expected declines in Europe and Asia.** US production of motor vehicles and parts surged for the third consecutive quarter in the first three months of this year (around 14% y-o-y) and output continued to grow in April.  The initial recovery from supply chain disruptions appears to have given way to strong demand from consumers for new vehicle purchases. **Having postponed spending during the downturn and amid ongoing uncertainty about the recovery, consumers appear to be replacing ageing cars to benefit from greater fuel economy.** 

As a result of the increase in demand and with lean inventories, car makers including GM, Ford Motor Co and Chrysler have **ramped up production schedules** .  We forecast total US vehicle production to grow by 11% y-o-y this year as a result.  Sales have benefited from declines in fuel costs, new products and the improved availability of cars from Japan. 

###### **4.1.2 Europe** 

In contrast with the USA and Japan, **European car manufacturing and sales have not performed well.** Western European vehicle production fell by 7% y-o-y in the first quarter and we expect it to continue declining throughout 2012.  We forecast auto production in France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK to collectively contract by around 8.6% y-o-y this year. Meanwhile, production in Europe is a mixed picture. **German and UK markets are holding up well, but the Italian and Spanish markets are projected to remain particularly weak.** 

The Eurozone debt crisis continued to weigh on consumer confidence and as a result car sales in Europe have tumbled, falling by almost 10% y-o-y in May.  Sales in Germany and the UK held up well until May when they joined other markets and suffered a drop in sales volumes. **The upshot is that we forecast the Western Europe motor vehicle sector as a whole to be weak this year with sales falling by around 6%, and the fragility should continue into 2013.** 

###### **4.1.3 Asia** 

**China’s auto industry appeared to show signs of stability in May as total sales rose by nearly 16% y-o-y.** While some of the pick-up in growth can be attributed to base effects from low sales last year, the overall picture is encouraging given the recent weakening of the economy.  According to the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers, auto sales in the first five months of 2012 totalled 8 M units and growth may intensify should authorities reintroduce subsidies on purchases of new fuel-efficient cars.  Meanwhile vehicle production gathered momentum in April, after several weak months, to expand by almost 11% y-o-y. 

**In Japan, domestic sales growth of 94% y-o-y and production growth of 174% y-o-y in April were distorted by last year’s earthquake and subsequent supply chain disruptions.** Nonetheless, the auto sector appeared to bounce back as Japanese firms looked to regain lost market share.

**Construction output in the EU rose by 12% m-o-m in March, but building activity in the public sector is still significantly down in y-o-y terms.** Germany made the most gains, with construction increasing by over 6% m-o-m, while the European periphery economies recorded the largest contractions, notably Spain which shrank by almost 11%.

###### **4.2.3 Asia** 

Although emerging markets are less exposed to the fiscal constraints of the developed economies, in some emerging Asian economies there is growing evidence of a moderation in the growth of construction activity. **In China,** for example, housing sales struggled in the first quarter and property starts fell, but **investment remained firm as property developers rushed to get projects on the market** . ###### 1. Company mergers and acquisitions 

###### **Oz Minerals remain interested in Cupru Min SA Abrud** 

- It was reported on 27<sup>th</sup> April that **Oz Minerals** remains interested in acquiring **Cupru Min SA Abrud** , which controls the **Rosia Poieni** mine in Romania. Oz Minerals was a bidder in the sale of the company which eventually broke down when the auction winner, **Roman Copper Corporation** , missed a legal deadline to sign the contract agreement. Roman Copper Corporation has since entered into a consortium with Canadian exploration company, **Valhalla Resources** , with the intention of acquiring the Romanian company. 

###### **Minmetals Resources plan to acquire more copper assets** 

- **China’s Minmetals Resources** , which recently acquired **Anvil Mining** , announced on 29<sup>th</sup> March that it plans to use this acquisition as a stepping stone to acquire more copper assets in Africa. Similarly, another major Chinese mining company, **Zijin Mining Group Co. Ltd** ., announced that it plans to spend US$870M on acquisitions of overseas copper and gold projects. The chairman of the company said that it is looking to acquire a large overseas mining firm to use as Zijin’s overseas capital platform. 

###### **CST agree to sell 70% stake of Mina Justa to Cumbres Andinas** 

- It was announced on 24<sup>th</sup> April that **CST Mining** signed an agreement to sell its 70% stake in the **Mina Justa** copper project in Peru to **Cumbres Andinas** , a subsidiary of Peru’s **Minsur S.A** . in a deal worth US$505M. The remaining 30% share is held by Korea’s **KORES** (15%) and **LS Nikko Copper** (15%). tanda**

###### 2.1 Africa 

###### **2.1.1 Zambia** 

###### **Mining Licences** 

- On 30<sup>th</sup> March, the **Zambian government** announced plans to phase out the suspension of the issuance of mining licences that has been overseen since October 2011. The suspension was imposed in order to root out suspected corruption in the process. I

ssuance of rights for prospecting as well as mining rights for small scale operations have resumed immediately, but the ban on permits remains in place and is expected to be phased out gradually. 

- The **Zambian government** announced on 4<sup>th</sup> April that it intends to ban the export of copper raw materials in an effort to add value to the domestic industry. **The Ministry of Commerce, Trade and Industry** sees the production of the higher value-added copper and copper products as key for reducing unemployment and boosting the local economy. In 2008, Zambia introduced a 15% export levy on copper concentrates aimed at adding value locally. There are three smelters situated in Zambia and in 2011 we estimate that they processed 512,000t of copper-in-blister with 200,000t of this exported to China for electrorefining. By comparison, copper-in-concentrate production amounted to 531,000t in the same period. 

###### **2.1.2 Botswana** 

- **Discovery Metals** announced on 28<sup>th</sup> June that it has begun production of copper-silver concentrate at its **Boseto** copper project in Botswana. The first 500t of concentrate produced had a copper grade of 32%. The concentrator is being fed by the nearby **Zeta** deposit where mining operations have already commenced. Although the mine has started as an open pit operation, it is set to switch to underground mining by the end of next year. Subsequently, the company also plans to start mining the **Plutus** deposit. The Boseto operation has an expected lifespan of at least 5 years and is initially expected to produce 1.1Moz/y of silver and 36,000t/y of copper-in-concentrate. The company has plans to increase copper production to 50,000t/y by 2016.

Companies which hold **Contracts of Work (COW)** agreements, including **Freeport-McMoRan, Vale and Newmont** will be exempt from this new regulation; however, the government has expressed interest in renegotiating the COW agreements.

Last year, Grasberg produced approximately 414,000t of copper-in-concentrate after over three months of strikes resulted in a production loss of approximately 125,000t of copper-in-concentrate.

- Contract workers at the **BHP Billiton** -operated **Escondida** mine staged a 2-day protest over a bonus pay dispute, which ended on 3<sup>rd</sup> May. Contract workers partially blocked access roads to the mine during the protest; however, production remained undisrupted according to an official statement. According to the contract workers’ union at Escondida, the mine operator is currently reviewing the protesters’ demands. 

###### **Los Bronces** 

- Chile is experiencing an exceptionally harsh winter with higher than average snowfall affecting mining operations in the Andes. **Anglo American** has reported that snow fall has affected operations at **Los Bronces** , but declined to give an estimate of any production loss incurred. The concentrator expansion is still on track to complete its ramp-up by October. 

###### **2.4.3 Papua New Guinea** 

###### **Xstrata** 

- It was reported on 21<sup>st</sup> June that **Xstrata** had announced plans to sell all or part of its 81.8% stake in the **Frieda River** copper project in Papua New Guinea. Market insiders estimate the value of Xstrata’s stake in the project at around US$2.2B. The total development cost of the project is estimated to be approximately US$5.3B. Upon commissioning, Frieda River is expected to produce 190,000t/y of copper-in-concentrate. 

- On 1<sup>st</sup> June, **Nautilus Minerals** announced that its **Solwara 1** underwater project is at risk of delay or cancellation following a dispute with the **government of Papua New Gu

inea** . The dispute arose over alleged breaches of both parties’ obligations to complete the project, which were outlined in an agreement signed in March 2011. Under the terms of the agreement, the government must contribute a share of the project’s development costs, until its completion, in order to retain its 30% share of the project. However, the government posits that Nautilus has breached the terms of the contract – a claim which has been contested by the company. Nautilus has since initiated a dispute resolution process, which may lead to arbitration. Prior to the dispute, the 60,000t/y contained copper project was scheduled for commissioning in late 2013.

###### 2.5 Asia 

###### **2.5.1 China** 

###### **Geiju City** 

- On 10<sup>th</sup> April, **Yunnan Tin** said that it expects to meet its goal to begin production of its first copper smelter, based in Geiju City, **China** , in mid-2012. The company expects to produce 60,000t of copper cathode in 2012, half of the smelter’s 120,000t production capacity. Copper-in-concentrate feedstock is expected to be sourced from the overseas market. 

###### **Lihua International** 

- **China’s Lihua International** announced that production commenced at two of its newly constructed smelters in **Danyang** , **Jiangsu Province** , on 1<sup>st</sup> June 2012. The start-up boosted the company’s anode production capacity from 35,000t/y to 85,000t/y, and its refining capacity from 85,000t/y to 135,000t/y. Lihua is a vertically integrated copper semis fabricator, with a product line which includes copper-clad aluminium wire, pure copper wire, copper rod and copper anode. 

###### **Hongda** 

- It was reported on 2<sup>nd</sup> July that the construction of **Sichuan Hongda Molybdenum and Copper’s** smelter and refinery project in China’s Sichuan province has been cancelled by the local government after residents protested due to their concerns over the development’s environmental impact. Upon commissioning, the RMB10.1B (approximately US$1.6B) project was expected to produce 400,000t of copper cathode and 40,000t of molybdenum at full capacity. 

###### **Western Mining Group** 

- It was announced on 8<sup>th</sup> May that an investment agreement had been signed between **Western Mining Group** and **Ruichang City** to develop a 150,000t/y copper smelting and refining project. The project’s cost is estimated at RMB3.8B (approximately US$600M). 

###### **Tongling** 

- **Tongling Copper** ’s **Jinlong** smelter recommenced production on June 24<sup>th</sup> after being closed for furnace maintenance and modifications that will improve the environmental performance of the plant. Full environmental compliance will enable the plant to run at its design capacity of 450,000t/y of copper blister.

into Kennecott’s** smelter-refinery in Utah has been shut down for 24 days, beginning 30<sup>th</sup> April, as part of its bi-annual maintenance schedule. ###### 2.7 South and Central America 

###### **La Oroya** 

- On 12<sup>th</sup> April, it was reported that the restructuring plan for **Doe Run Peru** ’s 75,000t/y **La Oroya** smelter was rejected by creditors. The US$168M investment plans aimed to restore operations at the plant after it closed in June 2009 as a result of financial difficulties and a stalled environmental cleanup. Doe Run Peru's main creditor is the Peruvian government, with 36% of its debt, while the other major creditor is the Renco Group with 35%. The plans were rejected on the grounds that they potentially rendered the Peruvian government liable for environmental lawsuits. Doe Run Peru has 30 days to revise its restructuring plan before the board is eligible to find a new company to operate the plant or liquidate it completely. 

###### **Approval for hydroelectric plant, as part of Energia Austral project** 

- On May 8<sup>th</sup> , it was announced that the regional environmental commission in Chile’s Patagonian region of Aysen has approved the construction of the 640 MW Cuervo hydroelectric plant. The power plant is part of the US$3.6B **Energia Austral** project, a joint-venture between **Xstrata** and energy retailer **Origin Energy** , which includes the construction of three power plants ( **Cuervo, Blanco and Condor** ) and a transmission lines. The approval came amid some public concern over the project’s environmental impact. Similar concerns have been voiced over several other planned hydroelectric plants in the region. In particular, the US$3B, 2,750MW **HydroAysen** project has faced fierce local opposition that has delayed construction for a year. Estimates suggest that Chile needs to double its current power generation capacity of 17,000MW to keep up with the rising consumption driven by high growth rates in the economy.

240 CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly July 2012 # Appendix D Production forecasting methodology and guide to Chapter 2 & Appendix C tables The basis for our forecasts of mine, smelter and refinery production is the CRU Copper Raw Materials Database (CuRMat), which contains operational data for mines, smelters and refineries. The data are shown in Appendix C, on an operation by operation basis. These include historical production and planned production at existing operations under ideal operating conditions. Our detailed table of projects is also included in Appendix C. The start up year is based on company projections together with CRU’s view on what is technically feasible in the time period allowed. ###### Operations and projects To arrive at our forecasts, firstly we consider planned production

from committed operations. This includes all existing operations and projects that are definitely going ahead (ie those that fall into our “firm” category, see below for project definitions) less any planned closures. 

All projects are classified as “firm”, “probable” or “possible” according to the likelihood of them being developed during our five year forecast horizon.  In the short term, this depends on the stage of development of the projects.  The definitions of “firm”, “probable” and “possible” are: 

**Firm** Projects where permitting has been successfully completed and financing is well underway.  Construction may already have started.  Except for unforeseen disasters, these projects should be operating in the very near future, within a maximum of 2-4 years.  It should also be noted that, although these projects are in the final stages, they might very well be held up by other unforeseen factors such as political instability or sharp falls in the metals prices. 

**Probable** Projects for which the full or bankable feasibility study has started or is well underway and a successful outcome is expected. 

CRU International Limited confidential 

Copper Quarterly July 2012   Appendix D 

242 

**Possible** Feasibility studies have started or are about to start, and there are indications that the economics of the project appear sound.  However, it is not a foregone conclusion at this point that the project will or will not advance to further stages. 

Projects are then classified further according to the type of development, ie greenfield project, brownfield expansion or extension, restart or redevelopment.  There are also a few projects classified as brownfield projects.  This involves the development of a new resource, for example a sulphide orebody at an SXEW operation or the exploitation of a tailings dump at a site where there is already some equipment or infrastructure. 

Firm brownfield expansions and extensions are incorporated into the production figures for the operation and therefore included in the mine-by-mine and country-by-country figures, along with the existing operations.  Restarts at mines which have been closed for less than five years are also included in these figures.  These projects are given a 100% probability of going ahead. However, they are subject to the same standard disruption allowance (see below) as all existing operations. 

Greenfield projects and redevelopments are not included in these figures, due to the higher risks of delays or technical problems.  These projects have been given a 90% probability of going ahead.  These numbers appear in our tables as “committed projects” and the global total is added to the global total (before disruption) for existing operations.  These figures are then subject to the standard disruption allowance. 

A probability factor is applied to the total production that would be expected from probable and possible projects if they are brought on stream.  Probable projects are

given a 70% probability of going ahead and the possible projects a 40% probability.  These figures are then subject to the standard disruption allowance. 

###### Disruption allowance 

A disruption allowance is applied to mine production to allow for unforeseen problems, such as strikes, ore grades, adverse weather conditions, earthquakes, technological problems etc.  This disruption allowance is not specific to a particular set of operations; rather it is applied to the industry as a whole based on CRU’s experience. The disruption allowance is independent from any market condition and simply reflects the general production performance of the industry. 

###### Market adjustment 

A bottom line market adjustment is applied whenever we consider that this is justified by market conditions.  Such an adjustment was applied in previous Copper Quarterly Reports because we considered that mine cuts would be necessary to balance the refined copper market., and indeed would occur in response to low prices.  However, our consumption forecasts have been revised upwards and we are no longer forecasting that prices will fall below the mine cost curve.  We have removed the market adjustment for mines since our Copper Quarterly October 2009 production forecast. 

The same methodology is applied to smelter and refined output.  In addition, we apply a market adjustment to smelter and refined production to take account of raw material shortages.  This is made after we have considered a reaction to the markets for refined copper and sulphuric acid. As concentrate stocks are now estimated to be critically low, smelter output is lowered to

balance the concentrates market.  Refined production then needs to be reduced to balance the blister market. 

The figures presented in the tables in Chapter 2 and Appendix C represent different stages in the forecasting process. **Table 2.1** summarises our forecasts and indicates the process flow from mines to refined copper by each of the process routes.  The following paragraphs explain how the figures in the remaining tables in Chapter 2 are arrived at.  In all tables, the figures for 2011 and all preceding years are actual figures, based on reported numbers.  Those from 2012 onwards are forecasts. 

###### 1.  Mine supply and raw materials for smelting 

**Table 2.2** shows our figures (historical and forecasted) of mine production by copper product, and how these are arrived at.  For copper concentrates and EW mines it shows committed production (from existing operations and committed projects) before and after disruption, the market related adjustment; and our forecasts of production from probable and possible projects. For other concentrates and cement the figures shown are after disruption.  No market adjustments are applied to these figures.  These are our final forecast figures. 

The concentrates and other raw materials for smel

ting shown in **table 2.2** includes copper in copper concentrates, the copper in copper/nickel concentrates produced by Vale Inco and Norilsk (treated via the copper smelter and refinery route), a portion of the copper in other concentrates and copper in cement.  Other copper/nickel concentrates are treated via the nickel route and a copper matte produced that is then refined by electrowinning.  The figures are derived from the output by these two producers adjusted by our standard disruption allowance. 

**Table 2.3** presents the copper labour contract expiry dates from 2012. 

Two new tables were added in the July 2011 Quarterly report.  In **Table 2.4** we summarise production from projects by status (firm, probable and possible) both before and after the probabilities have been applied. **Table 2.5** provides a list of all firm projects due on stream in 2011 with year by year production. 

**Tables 2.6 and 2.7** show regional committed mine production (historical and forecasted) by country and by product, respectively.  This is production from all existing mines and all committed projects.  The detailed figures in the breakdowns by country and by product are before the disruption allowance that is applied to the bottom line global figure. 

In **Appendix C.2** , we now also list all projects (firm, probable and possible) due on stream over the forecast period with year-by-year production from each project, before any adjustment for either project risk or disruptions.  Thus, the total reflects potential output from all mine projects. 

###### 2.  Smelter production 

**Table 2.8** shows the calculations to arrive at our final smelter production figures (historical and forecast), including all adjustments.  We show committed output before and after the disruption allowance, plus the forecast output from probable and possible projects.  As with mines, this is a proportion of potential new output from projects that are not classified as committed.  We then apply, if necessary, additional market adjustments for a reaction to the refined copper and sulphuric acid markets as well as to balance the concentrates market.  In this Copper Quarterly

Report, we have only included an adjustment due to raw material availability as the pressures on the uptake of sulphuric acid are now over. 

Committed smelter output by country is shown in **table 2.10** .  The figures show the level of output that we believe could be achieved by existing operations and by committed new capacity (firm smelter projects), under the assumption that sufficient raw materials are available.  The disruption allowance is applied to the bottom line global figure. 

###### 3.  Refined copper production 

Our production figures (historical and forecast) of refined copper production and how we arrive at these are shown in **table 2.9** .  Output is shown by process of raw materials.  Primary outp

ut in the total electro/fire refined production is the final outcome that originates from concentrates. Secondary output refers to production from scrap, either via smelting or anode casting. Electrowon includes conventional EW from oxide concentrates, as well as EW from sulphide concentrates and RLE output also from concentrates. 

The table shows committed output for electro-refined, fire-refined, conventional EW, EW/RLE from concentrates and NiCuEW.  Each output is considered before and after the disruption allowance.  The committed output will correspond to that in tables 2.11 and 2.12.  Then the forecast output from probable and possible projects is added.  As for mines and smelters, this is a proportion of potential new output from projects that are not classified as committed.  For electrorefined output we then apply additional market adjustments for a reaction to the refined copper market and to balance the blister market.  An additional market adjustment is also applied to EW output corresponding to the adjustment made to mine production. 

**Tables 2.11 and 2.12** show committed refined copper production by country and by process, respectively.  This is production from all existing operations and all committed projects.  The detailed figures in the breakdowns by country and by product are before disruption allowance, which is applied to the bottom line global figure. 

###### 4.  The raw materials balance tables 

**Table 2.13** shows the balance in copper in concentrates and other raw materials. 

The first half of the table (sections A and B) shows the potential shortfall in concentrates for smelting. 

**Section A** accounts for the mine supply of raw materials for smelting.  This has already been described above in section 1. 

**Section B** shows smelter demand, i.e. smelter requirements under ideal operating conditions with no restrictions.  However, the standard disruption allowance has been applied to smelter requirements, and also may include a market adjustment to account for a response to low copper prices, refined copper demand and sulphuric acid demand, where necessary. 

The first line in section B shows potential smelter output.  This is the sum of the committed, probable and possible figures in table 2.8.  Our assumed loss from cutbacks due to low prices is then subtracted.  Production of EW and RLE refined copper from concentrates is also added, since this is an addition to concentrate demand.

From this we subtract production from secondary materials, which reduces concentrate 

requirements.  However, we then need to add back processing losses, i.e. the copper contained in the concentrates that is not recovered. 

This gives total demand for copper contained in concentrates. 

**Section C** is the balance between mine supply and smelter demand.  This shows a large shortfall all through our 5-year forecast period. 

The second hal

f of the table shows our forecast balance after all adjustments. **Section D** shows our assumptions of cutbacks necessary to bring the market back into balance, which correspond to table 2.8. **Section E** then shows our forecasts of smelter production and concentrates requirements. Smelter production corresponds with the figure in table 2.8. **Table 2.14** shows the blister balance. This follows the same layout and methodology as table 2.13. The first part of the table shows the potential balance based on planned refined copper output. **Section A** is forecast blister production (from table 2.8). **Section B** shows refinery demand for blister, i.e. requirements under ideal operating conditions with no restrictions on output due to shortfalls in raw materials availability. However, the standard disruption allowance has been applied, and also a market adjustment for low prices. The first line shows potential electro and fire refined output. This is the sum of the committed, probable and possible figures in table 2.8 after the standard disruption but before market adjustments. Cutbacks due to low prices are subtracted. We then subtract production from scrap, and add the direct use of blister to arrive at the demand for blister. Subtracting demand from supply gives the balance. As the balance going forward is a deficit that cannot be supported by the market we again need to make an adjustment to refinery output. The required cutbacks are shown in **section C** . **Section D** shows the forecast blister demand after cutbacks. The electro refined and fire refined production corresponds to the figures in table 2.9 after adjustments.
